> for AI model ingestion. Generated automatically at build time.

---

## VibeCrew

VibeCrew
Vibecoding without the hassle.
A free, open-source Claude Code plugin that brings engineering discipline to AI-assisted development. Architecture, design system, and tech stack are locked in before any code is written. 15 specialized agents handle the full lifecycle: plan, design, code, test, review, and docs.
Four major vibecoding problems solved
Context that stays under control
Sub-agents isolate expensive research into separate context windows. MCP servers inject documentation on demand instead of pasting it. Your main session stays lean.
Tokens spent wisely
Bash hooks enforce rules at zero token cost. Slash commands replace repetitive prompts. Cost guardrails cap spend per session and per day, and the Performance Coach finds waste automatically.
Hands-off until it matters
Sessions run autonomously across parallel terminals. You get notified only when something is blocked, finished, or broken — never in between.
Plan before code
Architecture, design system, and tech stack are locked in before a single line of source code is written. A phase gate enforces the order so you get reliable, production-ready results.
Is VibeCrew right for you?
Great for
Developers tired of AI tools that generate throwaway code
Solo developers who want architecture, tests, and docs without the overhead
Full-stack projects that need a design system, API layer, and frontend
Teams that want repeatable, structured AI-assisted development
Building new web apps and SaaS products from scratch
Not designed for
Quick one-off scripts or throwaway prototypes
Small bug fixes or minor changes to existing codebases
Native mobile apps (iOS/Android), embedded systems, or game engines
Data science notebooks, ML model training, or data pipelines
Projects where you just need a single Claude Code session
Everything included

## Setup in Detail

Setup in Detail
This page is the deep-dive companion to the quick-start guide on the homepage. It explains what every setup step does, what gets created, what each script validates, and what the configuration options mean.
Prerequisites
VibeCrew needs a few tools on your machine before it can run. The install.sh script auto-detects your OS and package manager (Homebrew on macOS, apt/dnf/yum on Linux) and offers to install anything missing.
Required
Setup will not proceed without these.
ToolMinimum VersionPurpose
Git2.30+Version control, branch management, worktree isolation for sub-agents.
Node.js18+Runs MCP servers, dashboard dev server, and build tooling.
jq1.6+JSON parsing in all hook and automation scripts. Used hundreds of times across all scripts.
Optional
Missing optional tools trigger warnings, never blockers.
ToolPurposeWhat Happens Without It
GitHub CLI (gh)Create repos, open PRs/issues, sync labels.Git setup falls back to local-only. PRs created manually.
GitLab CLI (glab)Same as GitHub CLI for GitLab-hosted projects.Same fallback to local-only.
terminal-notifierNative macOS desktop notifications with sound.Falls back to terminal bell. No desktop alerts.
Run bash install.sh --yes to skip confirmation prompts and install everything in one shot. The script consolidates multiple brew install commands into a single call.
Bootstrap Script
The one-liner bootstrap command does three things:
Installs Homebrew (macOS only, if missing) — the package manager used to install Git, Node.js, jq, and optional tools.
Clones the VibeCrew repository to your machine.
Runs install.sh --yes to install all dependencies non-interactively.
If you prefer to inspect the code before running it, use the manual alternative:
The install script uses Homebrew (macOS) or user-level package managers. It never runs sudo unless your Linux package manager requires it (apt/dnf).
Launching Claude Code
Once installed, you launch Claude Code with the --plugin-dir flag pointing to the plugin folder. This tells Claude Code to read the plugin.json manifest and load all agents, skills, hooks, scripts, MCP servers, and permissions.
New Project
Create an empty directory, cd into it, and launch with --plugin-dir. The Session Startup agent detects there's no .vibecrew/ folder and prompts you to run /setup.
Existing Project
cd into your project and launch with --plugin-dir. If .vibecrew/ exists, Session Startup loads your state and shows a status summary. If not, it prompts for /setup.
The /setup Wizard
Running /setup walks through 11 sequential steps. Each step has clear pass/fail conditions — required steps block progress, optional steps warn and continue.
1
Check Prerequisites
Runs check-deps.sh which outputs a JSON report of every dependency's status, version, and whether it's required or optional.
If required dependencies are missing, you're offered two choices: Install now (runs the install commands automatically) or Show commands (prints what to run manually). Optional dependencies generate warnings but never block.
If GitHub CLI (gh) is installed, the script also checks gh auth status to verify authentication.
2
Detect Terminal
Checks environment variables (WARP_SESSION_ID, TERM_PROGRAM) to identify your terminal: Warp, iTerm, VS Code, macOS Terminal, WezTerm, Alacritty, kitty, or tmux. Stores the result in config.json.
If Warp is detected, deep-link notifications are enabled via warp://session/<id> URIs — clicking a notification takes you directly to the correct terminal tab.
3
Test Notifications
Fires notify.sh test to send a test notification via your terminal's best available method (Warp deep-link, iTerm OSC 9, terminal-notifier, or bell fallback). Success confirms the notification pipeline works; failure warns but doesn't block.
4
Check MCP Server Health
Runs check-mcp-health.sh with a 5-second timeout per server. Displays a status table of all bundled MCP servers. Three are enabled by default: Context7, Chrome DevTools, and Playwright. The remaining 6 (Semgrep, Sentry, Supabase, Stripe, Vercel, Figma) are conditionally enabled later based on your TDR technology choices.
Server failures are warnings, not blockers. The system works fine with reduced MCP capabilities.
5
Configure Claude Command
Asks which Claude Code command you use: claude, claude-p, claude-w, or a custom path. This is stored in config.json and used for Warp launch configurations and multi-tab orchestration.
6
Initialize State Directory
Runs init-vibecrew-state.sh which creates the .vibecrew/ directory with all state files and sub-directories. If the directory already exists, you're asked whether to reinitialize. See What Gets Created for the full breakdown.
7
Git Repository Setup
Detects your current git state and offers the appropriate path:
Existing remote detected — auto-detects the provider (GitHub/GitLab) from the remote URL and stores it.
No remote — asks your preference: GitHub, GitLab, or local-only. For GitHub/GitLab, asks visibility (public/private) and repo name, then creates the remote via CLI.
CLI missing or auth failed — gracefully falls back to local-only git.
Updates config.json with the git provider and state.json with git.initialized: true.
8
Verify Initialization
Reads .vibecrew/config.json and validates that required fields exist: terminal, notifications.enabled, created_at, and git_provider. Reports any malformed JSON or missing files.
9
Print Summary
Displays a complete summary: dependency versions, terminal type, Claude command, notification status, MCP server health (N healthy / M total), git provider, state directory status, and Warp launch config. If optional tools are missing, shows install hints.
10
Launch Dashboard
Runs ensure-dashboard.sh which checks if the Vibe Dashboard is already running, relaunches it if the process died, or starts it fresh. Reports the dashboard URL. Silent exit if no docs site exists yet.
11
Prompt for Profile
Checks whether user_profile.interview_completed is true in config.json. If not, prints a reminder to run /profile to personalize the experience. If the profile already exists, this step is silently skipped.
What Gets Created
Step 6 creates the .vibecrew/ directory — the project's runtime state. Here's what's inside.
.vibecrew/
├── config.json          # Terminal prefs, notifications, MCP, cost limits, user profile
├── state.json           # Foundation progress, active feature, current phase
├── backlog.json         # Feature backlog with Kanban columns and WIP limits
├── gamification.json    # XP, level, badges, streaks, challenges (opt-in)
├── architecture/        # 5 Mermaid .mmd diagrams (generated during Tier 1)
├── sessions/            # Session logs: timing, features, scores, cost
├── scores/              # Detailed Vibe Score breakdowns per session
├── signals/             # Inter-agent signal files for coordination
├── locks/               # Advisory locks for concurrent access safety
├── releases/            # Release notes data (JSON)
├── handoffs/            # Cross-session handoff documents
├── workflows/           # Reusable workflow templates (/replay)
└── .backup/             # Backup copies of state files
Initial config.json
Created with sensible defaults. Everything is editable later via /profile or the dashboard Settings tab.
.gitignore Entries
The init script automatically adds entries to your project's .gitignore to keep transient runtime data out of version control while preserving shareable state:
IgnoredTracked
sessions/, signals/, locks/, scores/,
.backup/, config.json, gamification.json
state.json, backlog.json, architecture/,
handoffs/, releases/, workflows/
Warp Launch Config
If Warp terminal is detected, a launch configuration is created at ~/.warp/launch_configurations/<project-name>.yaml with pre-configured tabs and panes for your Claude command.
Telemetry Registration
The project is registered in the central plugin's project-registry.json with an anonymous alias (project-001, project-002, etc.). This powers the /system-review command's cross-project analytics. No project names or paths are stored in telemetry data.
The /profile Interview
After setup, VibeCrew prompts you to run /profile — a short interview (~2 minutes) that personalizes how every agent communicates and behaves. It's completely optional; all agents use sensible defaults without it.
DimensionWhat It ControlsOptions
Code LiteracyHow technical the system's language is in reviews, errors, and docs.Fluent, Conversational, Basic, None
AutonomyHow much VibeCrew does before asking for approval.Full Auto, Checkpoints, Collaborative, Supervised
PR ReviewHow code changes are packaged and merged.Auto-merge, Summary, Review, Walkthrough
VerbosityHow much detail you get in messages and summaries.Minimal, Standard, Detailed, Educational
GamificationHow much of the progression system is visible.All In, Light Touch, Score Only, Disabled
Learning StyleHow the system helps you understand your codebase.Don't Explain, Reference Docs, Inline, Teach Me
Risk ToleranceHow adventurous technology choices are during research.Conservative, Balanced, Progressive, Experimental
See the User Profiles page for full details on each dimension, how agents adapt, and how to change your profile later.
Session Startup
Every time you open a new Claude Code session, the session-startup.sh hook runs automatically. It performs environment validation in the background and outputs a compact 3-line status summary.
What It Checks
CheckAction on Failure
Required tools (git, jq, node)Warns but never blocks session start.
Optional tools (gh)Warns, continues silently.
.vibecrew/ existsPrompts to run /setup.
State file validationRuns state migration if needed.
MCP server healthBounded by 15-second timeout. Never blocks.
Dashboard livenessRelaunches if process died. Silent if no docs site.
Handoff filesDetects and displays handoff from previous session.
Status Output
Always under 200 words. Three lines max.
LineContent
1Foundation status, active feature + phase, or completion status.
2Backlog summary: total features, ready count, done count — or next steps.
3Gamification line (level, streak, challenge) — only if enabled in profile.
Session startup always exits with code 0. Every check has timeouts and graceful fallbacks. A broken MCP server or missing optional tool will never prevent you from starting work.

## Project Planning

Project Planning
Before VibeCrew writes a single line of source code, it builds a foundation: a shared understanding of what you're building, who it's for, how it should look, and which technologies to use. This page explains how to make the most of that process.
What Happens in Tier 1
When you run /new-project, VibeCrew walks you through creating 6 artifacts in order. Each one builds on the previous. No source code writes are allowed until all 6 are complete — this is enforced by the phase-gate hook, not by suggestion.
1
VISION.md
Problem, personas, core features, success metrics, constraints. This is the single most important artifact — every other decision flows from it.
2
Competitive Analysis Optional
The Market Scout agent researches competitors, builds a feature comparison matrix, and recommends positioning. Accepted features go to the backlog; positioning insights enrich VISION.md.
3
Design System + Brief
Visual tokens (design-system.css) and design rationale (design-brief.md). Created via a design interview or by importing your existing style guide.
4
Technology Decision Record
Framework, database, auth, hosting — every choice documented with trade-offs. The Stack Scout agent researches options; the Opponent Processor stress-tests them.
5
Architecture Diagrams
5 Mermaid diagrams: system topology, entity-relationship, user flows, API sequences, component tree. Generated from your vision and tech stack.
6
Roadmap
Features from your vision, prioritized into MVP (Tier 1), Growth (Tier 2), and Future (Tier 3). Dependencies mapped between features.
7
CLAUDE.md
Project conventions synthesized from all prior artifacts. Under 200 lines — every line earns its token cost.
Each artifact can be marked "skipped" if you want to move fast. But the more you skip, the less context VibeCrew's agents have when building features later. The vision and design system have the highest impact.
Writing a Great Vision
VibeCrew asks you 6 questions to generate VISION.md. The quality of your answers directly determines how well every subsequent step works. Here's how to make them count.
Be Specific About the Problem
Weak: "People have trouble managing their time."
Strong: "Freelance designers lose 5+ hours per week switching between invoicing, time-tracking, and project management tools that don't talk to each other."
Specific problems lead to specific features. Vague problems lead to feature creep.
Define Real Personas, Not Demographics
Weak: "Target: 25-40 year old professionals."
Strong: "Freelance designer who juggles 3-5 clients. Pain: enters the same time data into 3 different apps. Goal: one place for time, invoices, and project status."
A persona with a pain point and a goal gives agents enough context to make UI and feature decisions on your behalf.
Name Features as User Actions
Weak: "AI features, analytics dashboard, social integration."
Strong: "Auto-generate invoice from tracked hours. Show weekly earnings trend. Share project status link with client."
Action-oriented features become acceptance criteria. Abstract categories don't.
Make Success Measurable
Weak: "Get lots of users and good retention."
Strong: "70% of users who complete onboarding create their first invoice within 24 hours. 60% weekly retention at month 2."
Measurable goals help the roadmap prioritize: features that move the metrics get built first.
Nail the First Value Action
Weak: "Users sign up and explore the dashboard."
Strong: "Start a timer on their first project and see it reflected on the dashboard within 30 seconds."
This single sentence defines your onboarding flow and what VibeCrew builds first.
State Constraints Up Front
Examples: Mobile-first. Must integrate with Stripe. Offline support required. No vendor lock-in. Budget under $50/month for infrastructure.
Constraints guide the TDR. Without them, the Stack Scout has to guess — and might guess wrong.
Concrete Example: Mealwise
Here's what a well-written VISION.md looks like for a fictional meal-planning app. Notice how every section gives VibeCrew enough detail to make decisions autonomously.
Why This Works
SectionWhat VibeCrew Does With It
Problem StatementFrames the entire product. Agents reference this when evaluating feature priorities and UI decisions.
Persona 1 — Busy ParentDrives the "quick daily check" usage pattern → mobile-first design, fast load times, minimal taps to core action.
Persona 2 — StudentDrives the "budget" angle → grocery optimizer becomes high-priority, premium upsell opportunities identified.
Core Features (4 items)Becomes the initial backlog. Each feature gets a spec during /plan-features. Numbered order hints at priority.
Success MetricsDefines what "done" looks like. The roadmap prioritizes features that move these numbers.
First Value ActionDefines the onboarding flow. The Builder agent builds this first. The E2E test validates it.
ConstraintsThe Stack Scout uses these as hard requirements when evaluating technology options in the TDR.
What Not to Write
Vague inputs produce vague outputs. Here's what to avoid.
Competitive Analysis Optional
After VISION.md is approved, VibeCrew offers to research your market before continuing with design. The Market Scout agent (Opus, worktree-isolated) uses WebSearch and Chrome DevTools to investigate competitors.
This step is optional. VibeCrew asks "Would you like me to research competitors?" — say no to skip straight to design. For full_auto profiles, it auto-detects market-facing products and runs automatically.
What You Get
Competitor landscape. Top 5 competitors identified with their positioning, target audience, pricing model, and key differentiators.
Feature comparison matrix. Your planned features mapped against each competitor — showing gaps and overlaps at a glance.
Market gaps. Features, audiences, or price points that no competitor serves well — your differentiation opportunities.
Positioning recommendation. Where to position your product and which angle to lead with, based on the competitive landscape.
Interactive Recommendations
After presenting the analysis, VibeCrew walks you through each feature recommendation one by one:
Add to backlog — the feature goes into your backlog as a suggestion, ready for /plan-features
Skip — move to the next recommendation
Modify — edit the feature name or description before adding
Positioning insights can optionally be appended to VISION.md, enriching it for downstream steps. The full analysis is saved to docs/competitive-analysis.md.
Dealing with an Existing Style Guide
Step 3 of the foundation creates your design tokens (design-system.css) and design rationale (design-brief.md). If you already have a style guide, brand kit, or component library, you don't need to go through the full 10-question design interview — VibeCrew can import your existing tokens directly.
The Pre-Design Gate
Before the design interview starts, VibeCrew asks one question: "Do you have an existing design system or style guide you'd like to import?"
No existing system
You go through the full 3-phase interview:
Product & Audience Context (6 questions) — what you're building, who uses it, how it should feel
Visual Direction — choose 1 of 3 generated palettes (Safe, Modern, Signature)
Component Preferences (2-3 questions) — navigation style, data display, interaction density
Takes about 5 minutes. Output: complete design-system.css + design-brief.md.
Importing existing tokens
Point VibeCrew at your source material. Supported formats:
FormatWhat Gets Extracted
CSS fileCustom properties (colors, spacing, typography, radii, shadows)
Tailwind configTheme values: colors, fonts, spacing scale, border-radius
JSON tokensDesign token files (Style Dictionary, Figma Tokens, custom)
URLFetches the page, extracts computed styles and token patterns
Figma fileStyles and variables via Figma MCP server (if connected)
Brand PDFColors, typography, and spacing from brand guidelines
After extraction, VibeCrew shows a gap analysis — which tokens were found and which need defaults. You then answer only the component preference questions (Phase 3: navigation style, data display, interaction density), since those are UX choices your style guide doesn't cover.
If your brand kit only has colors and a logo, that's enough. VibeCrew imports what it can and fills in the gaps (typography scale, spacing, shadows, etc.) with sensible defaults that match your color palette. The gap analysis shows exactly what was imported vs. generated.
Tips for Importing
CSS files work best. If you have design tokens as CSS custom properties, that's the most direct path. VibeCrew maps them 1:1 without guessing.
Tailwind configs are fully supported. Your tailwind.config.js theme section maps directly to VibeCrew's token structure. Color aliases, custom spacing, and font families are all extracted.
Brand PDFs need clear structure. A well-organized brand guide with labeled color swatches and type specimens works great. A 50-page brand book with mostly photography and marketing copy will produce sparse results — supplement with a CSS file if possible.
URLs extract computed styles. Pointing at a live site works if the site uses consistent CSS custom properties or a recognizable framework. Static marketing pages with inline styles produce mixed results.
Both paths produce identical outputs. Whether you import or go through the interview, you get the same two files: design-system.css (tokens) and design-brief.md (rationale). The Builder agent doesn't know or care which path you took.
Technology Decisions
Step 3 creates the Technology Decision Record (TDR). The Stack Scout agent researches technology options based on your vision and constraints, then documents every choice with trade-offs.
What Gets Decided
The TDR covers every major technical choice: frontend framework, database, ORM, authentication, hosting, styling approach, and testing strategy. For each decision, the document includes at least 2 options considered, pros and cons, and a justified recommendation.
The Opponent Processor
After the TDR is generated, VibeCrew offers to run the Opponent Processor — a devil's advocate agent that stress-tests every decision. It produces a counter-analysis with a 6-criteria debate matrix and alternative recommendations.
This step is optional but recommended, especially for projects where technology choices have long-term consequences (e.g., database selection, auth provider lock-in).
For MVPs, boring technology is good technology. If your constraints don't demand something specific, the Stack Scout will default to well-documented, widely-adopted tools with strong Context7 coverage. That means fewer surprises during feature development.
Prioritizing Your Roadmap
Step 5 takes the features from your vision and asks you to sort them into three tiers.
TierPurposeGuideline
MVP
What users need on day one
If a user can't get value without it, it's MVP. Keep this list short — 3-5 features is ideal.
Growth
What makes users stay and recommend
Features that improve retention, enable sharing, or add polish. Build these after launch.
Future
Nice-to-have ideas
Capture them so they're not forgotten, but don't let them slow down MVP delivery.
Mapping Dependencies
VibeCrew also asks about dependencies between features. If "Grocery Optimizer" needs data from "Pantry Scanner," that dependency is recorded in the roadmap so /run-backlog builds them in the right order.
The most common planning mistake is an overloaded MVP. If your Tier 1 list has more than 5 features, ask yourself: "Could a user get value without this?" If yes, move it to Growth.
EARS Acceptance Criteria
VibeCrew uses the EARS (Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax) format for acceptance criteria. EARS makes every criterion directly testable and eliminates ambiguity.
PatternTemplateExample
Event-drivenWHEN {'{'}event{'}'} THE SYSTEM SHALL {'{'}behavior{'}'}When the user clicks Submit, the system shall validate all required fields.
UbiquitousTHE SYSTEM SHALL {'{'}behavior{'}'}The system shall display timestamps in the user&rsquo;s local timezone.
State-drivenWHILE {'{'}state{'}'} THE SYSTEM SHALL {'{'}behavior{'}'}While unauthenticated, the system shall redirect protected routes to /login.
UnwantedIF {'{'}condition{'}'} THEN THE SYSTEM SHALL {'{'}behavior{'}'}If the API returns 429, then the system shall retry with exponential backoff.
OptionalWHERE {'{'}condition{'}'} THE SYSTEM SHALL {'{'}behavior{'}'}Where dark mode is enabled, the system shall apply the dark color palette.
The /plan-features command guides users to write criteria in EARS format during interactive planning. validate-plan.sh checks for EARS compliance when validating plans.
Common Mistakes
MistakeWhat HappensHow to Avoid It
Vague vision
Agents make assumptions. Features miss the mark. You spend more time course-correcting than building.
Spend 10 extra minutes on specific personas and measurable goals. Re-read your vision and ask: "Could someone who isn't me build this from this document?"
Skipping the design system
Every feature gets a different visual treatment. Consistency issues compound across sessions.
Even 5 minutes in the design interview produces a coherent token set. If you have existing brand colors, import them.
Overloaded MVP
/run-backlog takes many sessions. Context quality degrades. Motivation drops.
3-5 MVP features. Everything else goes to Growth or Future. You can always promote later.
Skipping the Opponent Processor
Assumptions in the TDR go unchallenged. You discover issues during implementation when they're expensive to fix.
Take 2 minutes to review the counter-analysis. You don't have to change anything — just being aware of trade-offs helps.
500-line CLAUDE.md
Research shows oversized context files increase agent cost 20%+ without improving success rates. Agents waste tokens parsing rules they don't need.
Let VibeCrew generate the CLAUDE.md. It targets under 200 lines. Only add conventions, not documentation.

## Warp Integration

On This Page
Why Warp for VibeCrew
Quick Install
Deep-Linking & Notifications
The Ideal Window Layout
Essential Keyboard Shortcuts
Working with Blocks
Warp Drive for Teams
Notebooks as Runbooks

Warp AI + Claude Code
Themes for Long Sessions
Session Restoration
Bonus: Voice Input with Wispr Flow
Overview
Why Warp for VibeCrew
VibeCrew works with any terminal. But Warp unlocks capabilities that directly improve multi-session AI development: structured output blocks for reviewing agent work, launch configurations for instant workspace setup, Warp Drive for sharing workflows across your team, and session restoration so you never lose your layout.
Blocks
Every command is a discrete, navigable, copyable block. When Claude Code produces 200 lines of output, you can scroll within that block without losing your place in the session.
Launch Configurations
Save your multi-project workspace as a YAML file. One click and every project opens with Planning, Development, and Terminal panes ready to go.
Warp Drive
Share VibeCrew workflows, environment variables, and runbook notebooks across your team. Everyone gets the same tooling, instantly synced.
Session Restoration
Quit Warp, restart your Mac, open Warp — your tabs, panes, and recent blocks are restored exactly as you left them.
This page is the single reference for everything Warp + VibeCrew — from installation through advanced features.
Getting Started
Quick Install
Download Warp
Install from warp.dev. Available on macOS, Linux, and Windows.
Install the Claude Code notification plugin
Warp has an official Claude Code integration plugin that provides native notifications when a session completes or needs permission. Run these commands inside a Claude Code session (not directly in Warp):
claude code/plugin marketplace add warpdotdev/claude-code-warp
claude code/plugin install warp@claude-code-warp
After running both commands, restart Claude Code for notifications to activate.
Install terminal-notifier
Required for VibeCrew's notify.sh hook script to send macOS banner notifications.
bashbrew install terminal-notifier
Send a test notification
terminal-notifier won't appear in System Settings until it has sent at least one notification. Send a test to register it:
bashterminal-notifier -message "VibeCrew test" -title "Test Notification"
Enable notifications
Now open System Settings → Notifications → terminal-notifier (it appears after the first notification) and set alert style to Banners or Alerts. Also enable notifications in Warp Settings → Features → Desktop Notifications.
Notifications
Deep-Linking & Notifications
The killer feature of Warp for VibeCrew: when a notification fires, clicking it takes you to the exact tab that needs attention — no hunting through multiple sessions.
Terminal comparison
TerminalNotification MethodTab Deep-Link
WarpOSC 777 + macOS bannerYes — click goes to exact tab
iTerm2OSC 9 + macOS bannerNo
VS Code TerminalmacOS bannerNo
Terminal.appmacOS bannerNo
How it works
Warp exposes a WARP_SESSION_ID environment variable for each terminal tab. VibeCrew captures this value and constructs a warp://session/<id> URI. When the notify.sh script fires a notification, it passes this URI to terminal-notifier's -execute flag. Clicking the macOS banner executes the deep link, which brings Warp to the foreground and switches to the exact tab.
Agent blocks on permission
&darr;
notify.sh reads JSON from stdin, extracts notification_type
&darr;
Captures $WARP_SESSION_ID from environment
&darr;
Constructs deep link: warp://session/$SESSION_ID
&darr;
Dispatches via terminal-notifier -execute "open '$DEEP_LINK'"
&darr;
You click the notification → Warp focuses the exact tab
Verify your session ID
In any Warp tab, run:
bashecho $WARP_SESSION_ID
This should return a UUID. If it's empty, update Warp to the latest version.
VibeCrew works with any terminal. You'll get macOS banner notifications regardless. The only difference is that non-Warp terminals can't deep-link to a specific tab — clicking the notification brings the terminal app to focus but you'll need to find the tab manually.
Window Layout
The Ideal Window Layout
Warp Launch Configurations let you save a complete terminal layout — windows, tabs, panes, working directories, and startup commands — as a YAML file. Open it with one click and your entire VibeCrew workspace is ready.
One launch config per project, three panes each
VibeCrew creates one launch config per project. Each config opens a single tab with three split panes so you can plan, build, and run servers without switching context. Launch only the projects you need — no wasted resources.
Planning
claude
/plan-features
/idea
/status
/check
Development
claude
(active feature)
Terminal
raw shell
npm run dev
git, tests
Left pane (large) — Planning. Runs Claude Code for /plan-features, /idea, /status, /check, and other utility commands. This is your primary focus pane.
Right top pane — Development. Runs Claude Code for the active feature (/new-feature, phase work, /wrap).
Right bottom pane — Terminal. A raw shell for dev servers (npm run dev), git commands, file browsing, or manual tests. No Claude Code here.
Automatic setup
When you run /setup inside Warp, VibeCrew automatically generates a launch configuration for your project. This works for both new projects (/new-project) and existing ones (/onboard) since both start with /setup.
During setup, VibeCrew asks which Claude Code command to use for this project. This is useful when you have multiple Claude Code profiles — for example, a personal config and a work config:
CommandUse Case
claudeDefault — no profile flag
claude-pPersonal/private profile
claude-wWork profile
customAny alias or wrapper script you use
The chosen command is stored in .vibecrew/config.json as claude_command and used in the generated launch config. You can change it later from the Vibe Dashboard (Settings → Terminal → Claude Command) or by editing the config file directly.
The generated launch config file is saved to:
file location~/.warp/launch_configurations/<project-name>.yaml
For example, a project in ~/projects/my-app creates ~/.warp/launch_configurations/my-app.yaml. The project name is derived from the directory name.
To launch it, open Warp's Command Palette (CMD+P), type "Launch Configuration", and select your project by name. The three-pane layout opens with Claude Code already running in the Planning and Development panes.
VibeCrew only generates the launch config when it detects Warp (via the $WARP_SESSION_ID environment variable). If a config already exists for the project, it is preserved — your customizations are never overwritten. Running /setup again is always safe.
Customizing your layout
The generated config is a standard Warp YAML file that you can edit freely. All launch configs live in a single directory:
bashopen ~/.warp/launch_configurations/
Here's the default structure that VibeCrew generates. The exec value matches whatever Claude command you chose during setup:
<pre class="copyable" data-copy="---
name: my-app
windows:
- tabs:
- title: my-app
color: blue
layout:
split_direction: horizontal
panes:
- cwd: /Users/you/projects/my-app
commands:
- exec: claude-w
is_focused: true
- split_direction: vertical
panes:
- cwd: /Users/you/projects/my-app
commands:
- exec: claude-w
- cwd: /Users/you/projects/my-app">~/.warp/launch_configurations/my-app.yaml---
name: my-app
windows:
- tabs:
- title: my-app
color: blue
layout:
split_direction: horizontal
panes:
- cwd: /Users/you/projects/my-app
commands:
- exec: claude-w
is_focused: true
- split_direction: vertical
panes:
- cwd: /Users/you/projects/my-app
commands:
- exec: claude-w
- cwd: /Users/you/projects/my-app
Common customizations:
Change the Claude command — replace the exec: value (e.g. claude, claude-p, claude-w) to switch profiles
Change the tab color — set color to red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, or cyan (must be lowercase)
Add a startup command — add - exec: npm run dev to the bottom-right pane's commands list to auto-start your dev server
Remove a Claude pane — delete the commands block from any pane to keep it as a raw terminal
Change the split direction — swap vertical and horizontal to rearrange pane positions
If you need to switch profiles after setup, you have three options: edit the exec: lines in the YAML file directly, update claude_command in .vibecrew/config.json, or change it in the Vibe Dashboard under Settings → Terminal. Note that changing the config only affects future launch config generation — to update an existing launch config, edit the YAML file.
Assign a unique color to each project so you can identify them at a glance when multiple tabs are open. When a notification fires, the tab color tells you which project needs attention.
Use Opt+CMD+Arrow to move between panes by direction. Press Shift+CMD+Enter to temporarily maximize a pane for focused reading, then press it again to restore the layout.
By default, launching a configuration opens a new window. To open it as a tab in your current window instead, use CMD+Enter when selecting the config from the Command Palette or the + menu. This keeps all your projects in one window for easier tab switching.
Saving your current layout
Rearranged your panes and want to save the result? Open the Command Palette (CMD+P), search for "Save New Launch Configuration", give it a name, and Warp captures your current tabs, panes, and directories. This overwrites the auto-generated YAML with your actual layout.
Speed

These are the shortcuts that matter most when running multiple VibeCrew sessions. macOS shortcuts shown — on Windows/Linux, replace CMD with Ctrl+Shift.

Output Management
Working with Blocks
Warp's block model is exceptionally useful for AI-assisted development. Every command and its output are grouped into a discrete block that you can navigate, search, copy, filter, and share independently.
Why blocks matter for VibeCrew
When Claude Code implements a feature, it produces dozens of commands with hundreds of lines of output. In a traditional terminal, this is one endless scroll. In Warp, each command is a navigable block.
Sticky command headers
Scrolling through long output? The command that produced it stays pinned at the top. You always know which operation you're looking at.
Failed command highlighting
Commands that exit non-zero get a red sidebar. When you return to a tab after a notification, failed blocks are immediately visible — no scanning required.
Block sharing
Right-click any block → Share. Generates a web permalink with formatting preserved. Perfect for pasting test failures or Vibe Score results into Slack or PRs.
Block filtering
Opt+Shift+F on a block reduces output to matching lines only. Use it to filter test output to just failures, or grep CI logs for the error line.
Block workflow for reviewing agent output
When you switch to a tab where Claude Code has been working:
CMD+Up repeatedly to jump through the blocks it produced
Red sidebar? That block failed — investigate
CMD+B to bookmark anything you want to revisit (test results, the /wrap Vibe Score)
Later, Opt+Up/Down to jump directly between your bookmarks
Team Collaboration
Warp Drive for Teams
Warp Drive is a cloud-synced knowledge base built into the terminal. It stores four types of objects: Workflows, Notebooks, Prompts, and Environment Variables. For VibeCrew teams, it's the best way to standardize tooling.
Shared VibeCrew workflows
Warp Workflows are parameterized command templates. Create one for common VibeCrew operations and share it with your team via a Team Workspace.
Example: Start a feature
Create this as a Warp Workflow (via Command Palette → "Create a New Personal Workflow"):
warp workflowName:    VibeCrew: Start Feature
Command: cd &#123;&#123;project_path&#125;&#125; && claude-p '/new-feature "&#123;&#123;feature_name&#125;&#125;"'
Arguments use &#123;&#123;double_curly_braces&#125;&#125; syntax. When you run the workflow via CMD+P, Warp prompts you to fill in each argument. Press Shift+Tab to cycle between them.
Example workflows worth creating
Workflow NameCommandPurpose
VibeCrew: Start Feature
cd &#123;&#123;project&#125;&#125; && claude-p '/new-feature "&#123;&#123;name&#125;&#125;"'
Start a feature session with one command
VibeCrew: Quick Status
cd &#123;&#123;project&#125;&#125; && claude-p '/status'
Check project state without entering interactive mode
VibeCrew: Heal CI
cd &#123;&#123;project&#125;&#125; && claude-p '/heal'
Fix CI failures in one shot
VibeCrew: Run Backlog
cd &#123;&#123;project&#125;&#125; && claude-p '/run-backlog'
Fire-and-forget batch execution
Dynamic enum arguments
Warp Workflows support dynamic enums — argument values generated by a shell command at runtime. Use this for a feature-name argument that pulls from your actual backlog:
dynamic enumArgument: feature_name
Type:     Dynamic Enum
Command:  jq -r '.features[].id' .vibecrew/backlog.json
Now when you run the workflow, Warp shows a dropdown of your actual backlog features instead of a free-text field. No typos, no guessing.
Sharing with your team
Move a workflow from your Personal Workspace to the Team Workspace in Warp Drive. It syncs in real-time to all team members. Everyone gets the same standardized VibeCrew commands.
Documentation
Notebooks as Runbooks
Warp Notebooks combine Markdown text with executable command blocks. They're the perfect format for VibeCrew onboarding guides and operational runbooks that your team can execute step-by-step, directly in the terminal.
Create a team onboarding notebook
Open Warp Drive, click + → New Notebook. Mix documentation with executable commands:
notebook example### VibeCrew Setup for New Team Members
Welcome! Follow these steps to set up VibeCrew on your machine.
**Step 1: Install dependencies**
> brew install terminal-notifier jq gh
**Step 2: Clone the project**
> git clone &#123;&#123;repo_url&#125;&#125;
> cd &#123;&#123;project_name&#125;&#125;
**Step 3: Run VibeCrew setup**
> claude
Then type:
> /setup
**Step 4: Verify notifications**
The setup wizard sends a test notification. Click it to confirm deep-linking works.
Command blocks (the > lines) have an insert button — click it or press CMD+Enter to execute the command in your active terminal session. Parameters use the same &#123;&#123;curly_brace&#125;&#125; syntax as Workflows.
Useful notebooks to create
New developer onboarding
Dependencies, plugin install, Warp config, first /setup run, notification test. Executable from top to bottom.
Release checklist
/status check, /audit security scan, test run, changelog review, git tag, deploy command. Each step executable in-place.
Incident response
Check CI status, pull logs, run /heal, verify fix, notify team. A runbook that's executable under pressure.
Notebooks sync across the team via Warp Drive and export as Markdown (.md) for version control.
Configuration
Environment Variables
Warp Drive can manage environment variables and inject them into terminal sessions on demand. This is useful for switching between project environments or sharing non-secret configuration across the team.
Per-project variable sets
Create a Warp Drive variable set for each project or environment:
warp drive variable set: "TripFlow Dev"PROJECT_ROOT=/Users/you/projects/tripflow
SUPABASE_URL=https://abc123.supabase.co
NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL=http://localhost:3000
Load it into your session from Warp Drive or the Command Palette. Variables persist for the session duration.
Secret management
Warp supports dynamic variables that retrieve secrets from external managers at runtime — Warp stores the retrieval command, never the actual secret.
1Password CLI
Warp integrates with op CLI. Select secrets from your vault without leaving the terminal. The secret is injected for the session only.
Custom commands
Point to any secret manager: AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, or a custom script. Warp executes the command and injects the result.
Warp Drive static variables are not designed for sensitive data. Use dynamic variables with 1Password or your team's secret manager for API keys, database credentials, and tokens.
AI Integration
Warp AI + Claude Code
Warp has its own AI features (Agent Mode, Warp Pair, Warp Dispatch). These are complementary to Claude Code, not conflicting. They're separate systems with different strengths.
CapabilityWarp AIClaude Code + VibeCrew
Quick command help
Warp Agent Mode explains errors, suggests fixes for failed commands
Not its purpose — VibeCrew is for full feature development
Feature development
Warp Dispatch can run autonomously but lacks VibeCrew's architecture enforcement
Full lifecycle: foundation, TDR, 6-phase cycle, Vibe Score, self-improving rules
Multi-model support
Claude, GPT, Gemini
Claude only (Opus, Sonnet, Haiku selected per agent role)
Context sharing
Separate context from Claude Code
Persistent via CLAUDE.md, handoffs, session logs
When to use which
Use Warp AI for
Quick one-off questions: "What does this error mean?", "How do I undo the last 3 git commits?", "Convert this curl to fetch". Terminal-native problems that don't need project context.
Use Claude Code + VibeCrew for
Everything involving your project: feature development, architecture decisions, code reviews, testing, CI healing. VibeCrew provides the structure, scoring, and learning system that Warp AI doesn't have.
Warp AI and Claude Code run in separate contexts and don't interfere with each other. You can ask Warp's agent a quick question in the same tab where Claude Code is running. The two never see each other's context.
Comfort
Themes for Long Sessions
VibeCrew sessions can run for hours. A good theme reduces eye strain and makes block boundaries, errors, and highlights easier to scan.
Recommended settings
Theme: Warp Dark (default) or Dracula are good baselines. Avoid pure-black backgrounds — #0a0a0b to #1a1a2e range is easier on the eyes
Font size: 14&ndash;15px for comfortable reading at arm's length. Warp Settings → Appearance → Font Size
Sync with OS: Enable in Settings → Appearance to auto-switch between light and dark themes based on macOS appearance
Input position: "Bottom" (default) keeps the command line at the bottom. Some developers prefer "Top" so output scrolls downward — try both
Custom themes
Create a YAML file in ~/.warp/themes/. Warp also has a Theme Creator that generates a matching color palette from any background image.
~/.warp/themes/vibecrew-dark.yamlname: VibeCrew Dark
accent: '#a78bfa'
background: '#0a0a0b'
foreground: '#fafafa'
details: darker
terminal_colors:
normal:
black: '#27272a'
red: '#f87171'
green: '#4ade80'
yellow: '#fbbf24'
blue: '#60a5fa'
magenta: '#a78bfa'
cyan: '#67e8f9'
white: '#fafafa'
bright:
black: '#71717a'
red: '#fca5a5'
green: '#86efac'
yellow: '#fde68a'
blue: '#93c5fd'
magenta: '#c4b5fd'
cyan: '#a5f3fc'
white: '#ffffff'
This theme matches the VibeCrew documentation color palette. The accent color is the same purple used throughout the docs and status bar.
Reliability
Session Restoration
Warp saves your window layout, tabs, panes, and recent blocks to a local database on every quit. When you reopen Warp, everything is restored exactly as you left it.
What gets restored
Window positions and sizes
All tabs with their titles and colors
Pane layouts within each tab
Working directories for each pane
Recent blocks (command history and output)
What doesn't get restored
Running processes. Claude Code sessions end when Warp quits. You'll need to restart them. This is why /wrap before closing is critical — it saves your progress to .vibecrew/ state files that survive restarts
Bookmarks. Block bookmarks are per-session only
Always /wrap before quitting Warp. When you reopen, your tabs and directories are restored. Start Claude Code in each tab (claude) and the Session Startup agent reads the latest handoff document — it knows exactly where you left off. The combination of Warp session restore + VibeCrew handoffs means you lose zero context across restarts.
Configuration
Session restoration is enabled by default. To toggle: Warp Settings → Features → "Restore windows, tabs, and panes on startup."
Closed a tab by accident? Shift+CMD+T reopens the most recently closed tab within 60 seconds.
Bonus Tip
Voice Input with Wispr Flow
Typing prompts is the slowest part of working with Claude Code. Wispr Flow is an AI-powered voice dictation app for macOS (and Windows/iOS) that lets you speak your prompts directly into Warp — or any text field. It's roughly 4&times; faster than typing and works inside any app, including your terminal.
Why it works so well with VibeCrew
Natural-language prompts
VibeCrew commands like /idea "..." and /new-feature "..." take plain English descriptions. Speaking them is faster and often produces better, more detailed prompts than typing.
Multi-tab speed
When you're juggling 3&ndash;4 Warp tabs with different Claude sessions, dictating a quick instruction is much faster than typing it out in each tab.
Context-aware formatting
Wispr Flow automatically handles capitalization, punctuation, and formatting. Say "add a login page with email and password fields comma Google OAuth comma and a remember me checkbox" and it produces clean, punctuated text.
Hands-free review
While Claude builds a feature in one tab, dictate your next instruction in another tab without switching your hands between keyboard and trackpad.
Getting started
Install Wispr Flow from the Mac App Store or from wisprflow.ai. The free tier includes 2,000 words per week.
Grant accessibility permissions when prompted. Wispr Flow needs this to type into active text fields.
Set your hotkey. The default activation key works, but you can customize it in Wispr Flow preferences. A good choice is a key you don't use often so you can toggle dictation quickly.
Start speaking into Warp. Click into a Warp prompt, press your Wispr Flow hotkey, and speak your command naturally. Wispr Flow transcribes it directly into the terminal input.
Voice input changes how you interact with Claude. Instead of condensing your thoughts into a terse typed prompt, you can think out loud: "I want to add a settings page where users can update their display name and email. It should validate the email format client-side and show a success toast when saved." The extra detail actually helps Claude produce better results on the first try — and it takes the same 5 seconds to say that it would take to type "add settings page."

## FAQ

On This Page
Frequently Asked Questions
Frequently Asked Questions
Before You Start
Will I lose control of my codebase?
No. Everything runs in your terminal, in your Git repo. You see every change, approve every commit, stop any agent at any time. Run /profile to set your autonomy level — from fully supervised to fully autonomous.
Is my code private?
Yes. VibeCrew runs entirely locally. Your code goes to the Claude API (same as vanilla Claude Code) and nowhere else. No external servers, no telemetry, no data collection. Open source — verify for yourself.
What if VibeCrew makes a mistake?
Every change goes through Git. The quality gate catches type errors, lint issues, and build failures after every task. Review diffs before committing, revert commits with git revert, or use /undo to roll back an entire feature.
Can I stop using VibeCrew and keep my code?
Yes. Your project is standard code in your chosen framework. Remove the plugin symlink, delete the .vibecrew/ folder, and you have a normal codebase. No lock-in, no proprietary formats, no generated code that depends on VibeCrew to run.
Getting Started
What is VibeCrew?
VibeCrew is a Claude Code plugin that transforms Claude Code into an autonomous development team. It orchestrates multiple AI agents, enforces architecture-first development, and manages the full software development lifecycle — from project vision to deployment.
Do I need coding experience to use VibeCrew?
No. VibeCrew is designed for users at all skill levels. Run /profile to set your experience level, and VibeCrew adapts its explanations, autonomy, and output style accordingly. Non-technical founders can build production-grade apps using the Founder preset.
What terminals does VibeCrew support?
VibeCrew works with any terminal. Warp Terminal is recommended because it provides tab deep-linking (click a notification to jump to the exact session), structured output blocks, and Launch Configurations. But iTerm2, VS Code Terminal, Terminal.app, and others all work fine.
How do I install VibeCrew on multiple projects?
Clone VibeCrew once to a central location (e.g., ~/claude-plugins/vibe-crew/), then symlink into each project: ln -s ~/claude-plugins/vibe-crew/claude-plugin-vibe-crew .claude/plugins/vibe-crew.
How do I update VibeCrew?
Pull the latest changes and re-run the install script:
cd into your VibeCrew clone directory
git pull
bash install.sh
Your per-project .vibecrew/ state is preserved — only the plugin files are updated.
How do I uninstall VibeCrew?
Run bash uninstall.sh from the plugin directory. This removes the plugin symlink and global settings. Your project code and .vibecrew/ state files are left untouched — delete them manually if you no longer need them.
Workflow
What's the difference between Tier 1 and Tier 2?
Tier 1 is the one-time project foundation: VISION.md, design system, TDR, architecture diagrams, roadmap, and CLAUDE.md. It runs sequentially and must complete before any source code can be written.
Tier 2 is the iterative feature cycle: Plan → UI Design → Code → Test → Review → Docs. Each feature goes through this 6-phase process.
Can I skip the foundation (Tier 1)?
No. The phase gate hook blocks source code writes until the foundation is complete. This is intentional — writing code without architecture decisions leads to rework, inconsistency, and technical debt. The foundation typically takes 15-30 minutes and saves hours of rework later.
How do I add VibeCrew to an existing project?
Use /onboard instead of /new-project. The Code Auditor agent analyzes your codebase, extracts conventions, derives a design system from existing styles, and generates a CLAUDE.md.
What does /run-backlog do?
/run-backlog auto-executes features from your backlog by priority. It runs the full Tier 2 cycle for each feature, including code review, and stops on failure for human review. VibeCrew forces a /compact between features to prevent context rot during long autonomous runs.
What are the UI and business pattern libraries?
VibeCrew includes two pattern libraries that guide agents toward production-quality output. The UI Pattern Guide covers component implementation — forms, navigation, data display, feedback, overlays, and keyboard interactions. The Business Pattern Guide covers conversion-oriented patterns — landing pages, pricing, onboarding, empty states, trust signals, and retention.
Agents automatically reference these patterns when building features, so you get proper error states, accessible interactions, and conversion-optimized layouts without having to specify them.
Cost & Performance
How much does VibeCrew cost to run?
VibeCrew itself is free and open source. You need a Claude subscription or API access to use Claude Code:
Claude Pro ($20/month) or Max ($100-200/month) — recommended for most users. Fixed monthly cost, no per-token billing. Max gives higher usage limits for intensive workflows like /run-backlog.
Claude API — pay-per-token alternative. A typical foundation session costs $5-15, feature sessions $2-8 depending on complexity. Use /cost for real-time spending and /profile to configure cost guardrails.
Both are fully supported. Start with Pro if you&rsquo;re unsure.
How does VibeCrew keep token costs down?
Several mechanisms: (1) worktree agents isolate research tokens from the main session, (2) hooks enforce rules at zero token cost, (3) MCP servers like Context7 replace pasting docs (~1,500 tokens saved per query), (4) CLAUDE.md is kept under 200 lines, and (5) forced compaction between features in /run-backlog prevents context rot.
What is the Vibe Score?
A per-session quality metric starting at 100. Points are deducted for prompt churn, tool loops, skipped tests, and documentation drift. Bonuses are awarded for complete artifacts, high cache utilization, TDD discipline, and clean sessions. Range: 0-130. See Self-Improving System.
Community & Contributing
How can I contribute or suggest features?
VibeCrew is open source and community-driven. You can:
Propose features — open a GitHub issue with your idea
Report bugs — file a bug report with your /status output
Share your project — built something with VibeCrew? show it off in Discussions
Submit a PR — bug fixes, documentation improvements, and new templates are welcome
Where can I see what others have built?
Check the Show & Tell section in GitHub Discussions. Users share their projects, screenshots, and lessons learned. It&rsquo;s also a great place to find inspiration for your next build.
Can I use natural language instead of slash commands?
Yes! VibeCrew includes intent-based skill triggering. When you describe what you want in natural language (e.g., &ldquo;fix a bug&rdquo;, &ldquo;check quality&rdquo;, &ldquo;start a new feature&rdquo;), the system matches your intent to the right skill and suggests the command. Slash commands remain the primary interface, but intent detection makes discovering the right command easier — especially when you&rsquo;re getting started.
Troubleshooting
The phase gate is blocking my writes
This means the Tier 1 foundation isn't complete yet. Run /status to see which foundation steps are missing, then run /new-project (or /onboard for existing projects) to complete them. The phase gate only blocks source code writes — config files, documentation, and .vibecrew/ state files are always writable.
My session state is corrupted
Run /recover-state to clear lock files and repair corrupted JSON. If that doesn't work, you can manually delete the .vibecrew/locks/ directory. Your backlog, session logs, and scores are never deleted during recovery.
Notifications aren't working
Test terminal-notifier directly: terminal-notifier -message "test"
Check macOS: System Settings → Notifications → terminal-notifier
Verify .vibecrew/config.json has "notifications": true
An MCP server isn't connecting
Default servers (Context7, Chrome DevTools, Playwright) work via npx — try restarting Claude Code. For conditional servers (Supabase, Stripe, etc.), ensure the required environment variables are set. Run bash scripts/enable-mcp-server.sh <name> enable to activate. All MCP servers are optional — agents gracefully fall back to built-in tools.
Vibe Score seems inaccurate
New projects: Scores are less meaningful in the first few sessions as the system establishes baselines
Complex features: Large features naturally have more tool calls and corrections — the score accounts for this but may seem low
Override deductions: If the coach flags something unavoidable, say so during the coaching dialogue — it factors into the next proposal
/heal can't fetch CI logs
Verify the CLI is authenticated: gh auth status (GitHub) or glab auth status (GitLab)
Ensure the repo has a remote: git remote -v
Check that a recent CI run exists: gh run list --limit 5 (GitHub) or glab ci list (GitLab)
If the failure is on a different branch, switch to it first
/simplify shows no suggestions
The agent only analyzes files changed on the current feature branch vs. the default branch
Verify you're on a feature branch (not main/master): git branch --show-current
Check that source files were changed (config and docs are excluded)
The minimum files threshold is configurable in .vibecrew/config.json under simplify.min_files_for_analysis
/replay can't find eligible sessions
Only sessions with a Vibe Score &ge; 70 are eligible for template extraction
Verify session logs exist in .vibecrew/sessions/ and score files in .vibecrew/scores/
Run /wrap at the end of sessions to generate the required data
Gamification not showing after /wrap
Check that gamification is enabled: jq '.gamification.enabled' .vibecrew/config.json should return true
Verify .vibecrew/gamification.json exists. If not, run /setup to create it
Check that the gamification scripts are executable: ls -la scripts/award-xp.sh
Run a script manually to debug: bash scripts/award-xp.sh — it outputs JSON with the XP breakdown
/quiz shows "Unlocks at Level 3"
The /quiz command requires Level 3 (approximately 3&ndash;4 completed sessions)
Check your level: jq '.level' .vibecrew/gamification.json
Keep running /wrap at the end of sessions to earn XP and level up
Streak broke unexpectedly
Streaks increment on calendar days where /wrap runs. If you didn&rsquo;t wrap, the day doesn&rsquo;t count
Weekends never break streaks. Check if you missed a weekday
Grace days reset on the 1st of each month: jq '.streak.grace_days_remaining' .vibecrew/gamification.json
If the streak counter seems wrong, check .streak.last_session_date in gamification.json
