## Daily Workflow

On This Page
A Normal Workday
Planning Features
Building a Single Feature
Running the Backlog Autonomously
Working in Parallel with Warp
Multi-Project Development
Monitoring Performance
A Full Week with VibeCrew
Best Practices
Deep Dives
Getting Started
A Normal Workday
Once your project foundation is in place, daily development follows a simple rhythm. Here's the mental model before diving into each use case.
Review PRs → Plan features → Build (manual or autonomous) → Monitor dashboard → Wrap up
Repeat. Each feature gets its own session and branch.
Morning: Merge yesterday's PRs. Check /status for open work. Mid-day: Build features — one at a time with /new-feature, or let /run-backlog handle multiple autonomously. End of day: /wrap every session, review Vibe Scores, capture stray ideas with /idea.
The rest of this page covers each part in detail.
Use Case
Planning Features
"I have ideas and need to turn them into buildable specs."
/idea — instant capture
Ideas come at the worst times — mid-implementation, during testing, while reviewing code. Capture them instantly without losing flow. One line in, one line out, zero context consumed.
any tab> /idea "add dark mode toggle to settings page"
Added to backlog: "add dark mode toggle to settings page" (unplanned)
> /idea "export trip itinerary as PDF"
Added to backlog: "export trip itinerary as PDF" (unplanned)
> /idea "rate limiting on auth endpoints"
Added to backlog: "rate limiting on auth endpoints" (unplanned)
Ideas land in .vibecrew/backlog.json with status "unplanned". They sit there until your next planning session.
/plan-features — structured specs
When you've accumulated several ideas, run /plan-features to promote them to structured specs. VibeCrew reads your roadmap and walks through each feature. For each one, you provide or confirm:
Name and description — one sentence
Acceptance criteria — when is this feature "done"?
Priority — P0 (must have) through P3 (nice to have)
Complexity — trivial / standard / complex (determines which phases run)
Dependencies — which features must exist first?
Planning session$ claude
VibeCrew v1.0.0 | Foundation: complete | No active feature
Ready. 5 features in roadmap, 0 planned.
> /plan-features
The output is .vibecrew/backlog.json — a structured file that /new-feature and /run-backlog read to determine what to build next.
Planning session> /wrap
Vibe Score: 92/100
5 features planned. Backlog ready for /new-feature or /run-backlog.
Weekly planning ritual
Every week, ideas accumulate via /idea. Process them before they become a graveyard of forgotten thoughts.
Every Friday (or Monday morning):
1. Run /status to see the full picture
2. Run /plan-features to promote unplanned ideas to specs
3. Review Vibe Score trends — are scores going up or down?
4. Review CLAUDE.md rules added by Performance Coach
5. Merge any remaining PRs
6. /wrap to close the week
Total: ~30 minutes. Sets up the entire next week.
Use Case
Building a Single Feature
"I want to build one feature with full control."
/new-feature "name" creates a feature branch and initializes 6-phase tracking. Each feature passes through: Plan → UI Design → Code → Test → Review → Docs. Here's a complete walkthrough building "User Authentication".
Starting the feature
Development$ claude
VibeCrew v1.0.0 | Foundation: complete | No active feature
Next in backlog: user-auth (P0, M complexity)
> /new-feature "user-auth"
Created branch: feat/user-auth
Loaded spec from backlog. 6-phase tracking initialized.
Phases: [ ] Plan  [ ] UI Design  [ ] Code  [ ] Test  [ ] Review  [ ] Docs
The 6 phases
Phase 1: Plan (~3 min)
Development> "Plan the user authentication feature"
Writing implementation plan at docs/features/user-auth/plan.md
Exploring existing codebase...
- src/middleware.ts: existing middleware, needs auth check added
- src/lib/supabase: client exists, server module needed
Approach: Supabase Auth with SSR helpers
Files to create: 5 new, 2 modified
Testing approach: spec-first for auth logic, impl-first for UI
Discuss: 4 decisions classified
| Locked     | OAuth providers?  | Google + GitHub          | Spec      |
| Locked     | Session timeout?  | 24h default              | User      |
| Discretion | Error toast style? | Shadcn Sonner           | Builder   |
| Deferred   | i18n support?     | Revisit in phase 2       | Spec TBD  |
Structured tasks: 5 tasks generated
Phase complete: Plan
Phases: [x] Plan  [ ] UI Design  [ ] Code  [ ] Test  [ ] Review  [ ] Docs
The Discuss phase (Clarify sub-step) runs automatically within Plan for standard and complex features. It evaluates 6 categories of potential ambiguities (Layout, Data, Content, Interaction, Business Logic, Integration) and classifies every decision into three categories:
CategoryMeaningCode Phase Behavior
LockedExplicitly in spec, TDR, or user answerFollow exactly. Deviation requires plan revision.
DeferredIntentionally left open (&ldquo;TBD&rdquo;, &ldquo;later&rdquo;)Skip. Add TODO(deferred) comment in code.
DiscretionSpec silent, doesn&rsquo;t affect acceptance criteriaBuilder picks best option; documents rationale.
Your /profile autonomy setting controls which decisions need your input: full_auto auto-resolves everything, while collaborative pauses for ambiguous items that could be Locked. Structured tasks (Files/Action/Verify/Done) give the Code phase a deterministic checklist to follow.
Plan Verification Loop
After generating the implementation plan, the Builder runs a pre-execution verification loop (max 3 iterations) via verify-plan-goals.sh. This catches requirement gaps before tokens are spent on implementation.
CheckWhat It ValidatesBlocking?
Goal CoveragePlan tasks address all acceptance criteriaYes
Dependency IntegrityReferenced files exist for &ldquo;modify&rdquo; actionsYes
Context BudgetEstimated context usage within 40% thresholdNo (warning)
EARS FormatAcceptance criteria use EARS syntaxNo (advisory)
Nyquist Test Coverage Mapping — After verification, the Builder maps existing test coverage to acceptance criteria. Criteria without matching tests generate Wave 0 tasks (test scaffolding) that are inserted before implementation tasks. This ensures test infrastructure exists before code is written. See Testing for details.
Plan Freshness Check — Before the Code phase begins, VibeCrew automatically checks whether any files referenced in your plan have changed since planning completed (from other features, quick fixes, or dependency updates). Minor changes are noted and the affected files are re-read. Major changes trigger a plan refresh for the affected tasks. This prevents building against stale assumptions.
Phase 2: UI Design (~5 min)
Development> "Design the auth UI components"
Generating ASCII wireframe for auth pages...
┌─ /login ────────────────────────┐
│  ┌─ AuthLayout (centered) ────┐ │
│  │  Logo                      │ │
│  │  [Input: email]            │ │
│  │  [Input: password]         │ │
│  │  [Button: "Sign In"]       │ │
│  │  ── or ──                  │ │
│  │  [Button: "Google"]        │ │
│  │  Link: "Create account"    │ │
│  └────────────────────────────┘ │
└─────────────────────────────────┘
Here's the proposed layout. Any changes before I write the design spec?
> "Move OAuth buttons above the form"
[Wireframe redrawn with OAuth buttons at top]
Writing design spec with wireframes at docs/features/user-auth/design.md
Phase complete: UI Design
Phases: [x] Plan  [x] UI Design  [ ] Code  [ ] Test  [ ] Review  [ ] Docs
Wireframes let you verify the layout before any code is written. Iterating on cheap text diagrams (&sim;50 tokens each) instead of rebuilding code (&sim;500-2000 tokens per cycle) reduces alignment-related rework by 70-90%. In interactive mode, you can say things like "make the sidebar narrower" or "add a search bar to the header".
Phase 3: Code (~15 min)
The longest phase. The Builder agent writes the implementation, consulting Context7 for Supabase and Next.js APIs instead of guessing.
Development> "Implement user authentication"
Builder agent activated. Working within TDR boundaries.
Checking Context7 for Supabase Auth API...
Creating src/lib/supabase/client.ts
Creating src/lib/supabase/server.ts
Creating src/app/(auth)/login/page.tsx
Creating src/app/(auth)/signup/page.tsx
Creating src/middleware.ts
Creating src/components/auth/LoginForm.tsx
Creating src/components/auth/SignupForm.tsx
Creating src/components/auth/OAuthButtons.tsx
Phase complete: Code
Phases: [x] Plan  [x] UI Design  [x] Code  [ ] Test  [ ] Review  [ ] Docs
While building auth, you realize you'll need a "forgot password" flow. Don't start building it — that's scope creep. Capture it instantly with /idea "forgot password flow with email reset link" and get back to work. One line, zero context spent.
Phase 4: Test (~8 min)
Development> "Write tests for user authentication"
Writing tests (TDD-hybrid approach):
Creating src/__tests__/auth/login.test.tsx
Creating src/__tests__/auth/signup.test.tsx
Creating src/__tests__/auth/middleware.test.ts
Running test suite...
12 tests passed, 0 failed
Phase complete: Test
Phases: [x] Plan  [x] UI Design  [x] Code  [x] Test  [ ] Review  [ ] Docs
Phase 5: Review (~3 min)
Development> /review
Code Reviewer agent activated (read-only worktree).
Reviewing against: feature spec, TDR constraints, project conventions
Checking TDR compliance... OK
Checking conventional commit format... OK
Checking design system token usage... OK
1 warning: LoginForm missing aria-live region for error messages
Phase complete: Review
Phases: [x] Plan  [x] UI Design  [x] Code  [x] Test  [x] Review  [ ] Docs
Phase 6: Docs (~2 min)
Development> "Generate documentation for user auth"
Updating CHANGELOG.md
Updating docs/features/user-auth.md with implementation notes
Session log saved to .vibecrew/sessions/
Phase complete: Docs
Phases: [x] Plan  [x] UI Design  [x] Code  [x] Test  [x] Review  [x] Docs
Wrapping up
Development> /wrap
Running quality gate...
Build: passed
Tests: 12/12 passed
Lint: 0 errors
Types: 0 errors
Performance Coach analysis:
Vibe Score: 91/100
Deductions: -5 (1 prompt refinement), -4 (minor context overhead)
Coaching: "Consider writing test stubs before implementation
next time to catch edge cases earlier."
Proposed CLAUDE.md rule: "Write test file stubs with describe
blocks before implementing features."
Accept rule? (y/n)
> y
Rule added to CLAUDE.md [Session Learnings].
Committed: feat(auth): implement user authentication
Branch feat/user-auth ready for PR.
One feature per session. Each Claude Code session has a finite context window. Cramming two features into one means both get less attention and lower Vibe Scores. Commit at phase boundaries. Each phase completion is a natural commit point — if something goes wrong later, you can roll back to the last clean phase. Use /check mid-session to run the full quality gate (build, tests, lint, types) without wrapping up.
Use Case
Running the Backlog Autonomously
"I want VibeCrew to build multiple features while I do other things."
/run-backlog automates the full 6-phase cycle for each feature in your backlog. It picks up the next planned feature, builds it through all phases, wraps it, and moves to the next one.
Development> /run-backlog
Starting autonomous backlog run.
3 features queued: trip-creation, itinerary-builder, group-invites
Building: trip-creation...
Complexity-aware processing
/run-backlog respects each feature's complexity setting. Trivial features skip Design and Review phases for faster throughput. Complex features with milestones use wave-based execution — independent milestones run in parallel via separate Agent calls, each with its own fresh context window. If Agent delegation is unavailable, milestones fall back to sequential processing with /compact between them.
Parallel mode (--parallel)
Add --parallel to process independent features simultaneously:
/run-backlog --parallel. VibeCrew analyzes feature dependencies and groups
features into waves. Features within the same wave have no dependencies on
each other and can be built concurrently (up to
max_parallel_agents from config.json, default 3). Each parallel feature runs
as a concurrent Agent tool call within the same parent session — not a separate Claude Code
session. Every Agent gets its own fresh context window and isolated git worktree. Waves are processed
sequentially — Wave 2 only starts after all Wave 1 features are merged and pass
the quality gate. See Advanced Features for details.
Fresh-session execution
Each feature is executed in a completely fresh 200k context window via Agent tool delegation. The orchestrating /run-backlog session prepares a context bundle (feature spec + TDR + architecture + design system + CLAUDE.md + profile + analysis docs) and spawns a Builder agent with it. This eliminates context rot entirely — feature 5 gets the same quality as feature 1. If Agent delegation is unavailable, VibeCrew falls back to inline execution with /compact between features.
When to use /run-backlog vs /new-feature
/run-backlog
Features are well-specced with clear acceptance criteria. You trust VibeCrew to make implementation decisions. You want to batch-build multiple features while you do other work.
/new-feature
The feature needs creative direction or nuanced decisions. You want to guide each phase. You're learning the workflow and want to see each step.
What to expect
VibeCrew notifies you on three conditions only: permission prompts (a tool needs approval), task completion (a feature finished), and critical failures (something broke). Everything else runs silently. You'll get a native OS notification for each — click it to jump directly to the session.
Use Case
Quick Fixes
"I just need to fix a typo / tweak a config value / update some copy."
/quick "description" is a lightweight alternative to the full feature lifecycle. It skips planning, design, review, and docs — just code the fix, run the quality gate, and commit.
Development> /quick "fix typo in pricing page header"
Locating file...
src/app/pricing/page.tsx: "Prcing" → "Pricing"
Quality gate: build ✓  lint ✓  types ✓  tests ✓
Committed: fix(pricing): fix typo in pricing page header (abc1234)
What /quick does NOT do
No backlog entry — visible in git log and session log only
No feature branch — commits directly to the current branch
No state mutation — doesn't interfere with in-progress features
No Vibe Score — too lightweight to score
Scope guard
If your description sounds like a feature (mentions "new page", "migration", "endpoint", etc.), VibeCrew will suggest /new-feature instead. You can override and proceed if you're sure it's a small change.
Use Case
Working in Parallel with Warp
"I want to plan ahead while a feature builds."
VibeCrew is designed for parallel work across multiple terminal panes. Each project gets its own Warp tab with three split panes.
Left — Planning
claude
/plan-features, /idea
/status, /check, /cost
Right top — Development
claude
Building: user-auth
Code phase active
Right bottom — Terminal
npm run dev
Local server running
http://localhost:3000
Left: Planning
Your primary focus. /plan-features to refine upcoming specs, /idea to capture thoughts, /status to check progress, /check to run quality gates.
Right top: Development
The one in-progress feature moves through the 6 phases here. Guide decisions, review output, run /wrap when done.
Right bottom: Terminal
A raw shell for npm run dev, git commands, manual tests, or quick file browsing. Not a Claude Code session.
How a multi-pane session flows
9:00  Development pane: /new-feature "trip-creation"
Terminal pane: npm run dev
9:05  Development: You guide the Plan phase for trip-creation.
Planning: /plan-features — refine the itinerary-builder spec.
9:25  Development: Code phase starts. Builder agent working.
Planning: /idea "add map view to itinerary with Mapbox"
9:30  Notification: "Development pane — Code phase complete."
You review the code, start the Test phase.
9:45  Development: All phases done. /wrap → Score 88
WIP slot is now free.
9:46  Development: /new-feature "itinerary-builder"
Spec is already polished from earlier planning — Plan phase is fast.
10:15 Development: /wrap → Score 85
Two features shipped in ~75 minutes.
Only one feature can be in-progress at a time. This is enforced at multiple levels: state.json tracks a single active feature, backlog.json limits the in-progress column to 1, and claim-task.sh blocks new claims. This prevents merge conflicts, keeps context focused, and produces higher Vibe Scores.
You don't need to watch all panes. The Interrupt Protocol sends a native OS notification when any session needs you (permission prompt, task complete, or error). Click the notification to jump directly to that pane. Work in your Planning pane until you're interrupted — that's the whole system.
For Warp installation, launch configurations, and keyboard shortcuts, see the Warp Integration page.
Use Case
Multi-Project Development
"I'm working on 2+ projects simultaneously."
Each project gets its own Warp tab with the same 3-pane layout. Color-code tabs so you can identify projects at a glance.
CMD+1 through CMD+8 to jump between projects
Opt+CMD+Arrow to move between panes within a tab
Every pane with Claude Code runs its own context window. They share the filesystem (git branches, .vibecrew/ state, CLAUDE.md) but not conversation history. This is by design — planning in one pane doesn't consume context in the development pane. Coordinate between sessions via branches: each feature gets its own branch.
Use Case
Monitoring Performance
"I want to check how my sessions are going."
Vibe Dashboard
A browser-based metrics dashboard showing your Kanban board, Vibe Score trends, and session logbook. Launch it with:
Terminal$ bash scripts/start-dashboard.sh
The dashboard shows feature status (backlog/in-progress/done), score trends over time, and detailed session logs. See the Dashboard page for a full tab-by-tab reference.
/status — quick CLI check
For a quick look without leaving the terminal:
any tab> /status
Open PRs:
#12 feat/user-auth        — approved, ready to merge
#13 feat/trip-creation    — review requested, 2 days old
#14 feat/itinerary-builder — draft, tests passing
Context usage: 42%
Features: 3/5 complete | Backlog: 2 planned, 4 ideas
Context budget
The check-context.sh hook warns at 45% and 60% context usage. Don't wait for the warning — check proactively with /status.
Above 70%, Claude Code starts losing early conversation context. It may forget design decisions, repeat questions, or generate contradictory code. The rule: if you're past 60%, wrap up and start fresh. A new session with full context is always better than pushing a depleted one.
Vibe Score
Every session ends with a score (0&ndash;100) calculated from real work artifacts. Starts at 100, applies deductions for prompt churn, tool loops, low cache utilization, missing tests, skipped reviews, and documentation drift. Bonuses for clean sessions, high test coverage, TDD discipline, and complete phase artifacts. The Performance Coach proposes permanent CLAUDE.md rule mutations based on patterns it detects.
Putting It Together
A Full Week with VibeCrew
Here's what a productive week looks like building a travel planning SaaS called TripFlow from zero to a working MVP.
Monday: Foundation
1 tab, 1 session. Run /new-project. Complete all 6 foundation steps. Run /plan-features to spec out your first 5 features. End with /wrap. Total: ~45 min.
Tuesday: First features
1 tab, 2 sessions. Build user-auth in session 1. Build trip-creation in session 2. /wrap after each. Capture 3 ideas with /idea along the way. Total: ~2 hours.
Wednesday: Full 3-pane workflow
3 panes. Build itinerary-builder in Development while planning group-invites in Planning. Dev server running in Terminal. Once itinerary-builder wraps, start group-invites immediately — spec is already polished. Total: ~2 hours, 2 features.
Thursday: Final feature + cleanup
3 panes. Development: Build expense-splitting. Planning: Run /simplify on earlier features. Run /heal if CI has issues. Total: ~1.5 hours.
Friday: Polish + review
1 tab. Run /status. Review Vibe Score trends. Plan next week from captured ideas. Review and merge PRs. /wrap to close the week. Total: ~1 hour.
Week summary
Features shipped:  5 (user-auth, trip-creation, itinerary-builder, group-invites, expense-splitting)
Sessions:           8
Average Vibe Score: 89
Ideas captured:     12 (ready for next week's /plan-features)
CLAUDE.md rules:    3 new rules added by Performance Coach
Total active time:  ~8 hours across 5 days
Week 2 is faster than Week 1. The 3 CLAUDE.md rules from this week prevent token waste next week. Your /replay templates capture what worked. The Performance Coach learns your patterns. By Week 4, you're shipping at nearly double the pace — not because you're working harder, but because the system is eliminating waste automatically.
Feature Management
Pause & Resume
Need to switch context? /pause checkpoints your current feature so you can safely start something else, then /resume picks up exactly where you left off.
Mid-Feature> /pause
Feature paused: user-authentication (feat-003)
Phase: code
Branch: feat/user-authentication (preserved)
Handoff: .vibecrew/handoffs/pause-feat-003.md
Worktree: cleaned up
Run /resume to continue this feature in a new session.
New Session> /resume
Feature resumed: user-authentication (feat-003)
Phase: code
Branch: feat/user-authentication
Worktree: recreated
Continuing at the code phase. Ready to work.
What happens during /pause:
Uncommitted changes are committed as a WIP checkpoint
A structured handoff file captures the full context
The feature branch is preserved (never deleted)
The worktree is optionally cleaned up to free disk space
Session Startup detects paused features and suggests /resume
Quick Reference
Best Practices
VibeCrew enforces many rules automatically through hooks, but some habits need to be built by you.
1. Always /wrap before closing a tab
2. One feature per session, no exceptions
3. Review & merge PRs before building more features
4. Wrap up at 60% context — don't push past it
5. Run /plan-features weekly to process ideas
6. Commit at every phase boundary
7. Keep .vibecrew/ in version control
8. Never build on main — always use feature branches
9. Resolve uncommitted changes before starting new work
10. Let Session Startup detect stale sessions
11. Use ASCII wireframes to align on layout before code
12. Set complexity during /plan-features to right-size the workflow
The phase gate blocks writes on main. Session Startup detects stale sessions and uncommitted changes. The context hook warns at 45% and 60%. /new-feature creates branches automatically. The habits above are about the few things only you can do — like remembering to /wrap and reviewing PRs.

Advanced
Advanced Workflows
VibeCrew includes four advanced workflows that extend the development lifecycle: reusable session templates, automated code simplification, self-healing CI, and adversarial review of technology decisions.
Workflow Templates (/replay)
Capture what worked and reuse it. /replay extracts reusable workflow templates from successful sessions (Vibe Score &ge; 70) so you can apply proven patterns to future features.
Three modes
List templates
Run /replay with no arguments to list all saved workflow templates with their names, descriptions, and quality thresholds.
Create a template
Run /replay --create <name> to extract a template from the most recent high-scoring session. Captures phase order, branch conventions, test strategy, and quality thresholds.
Apply a template
Run /replay <name> to load a template and have it guide your current feature development with the proven workflow.
After a session scores 90+, create a template. Common examples: "api-feature" for CRUD endpoints, "ui-component" for design-system-aligned components, "data-migration" for schema changes. Templates are stored in .vibecrew/workflows/.
Code Simplification (/simplify)
After building a feature, run /simplify to get an Opus-powered analysis of your code for unnecessary complexity. The agent operates in a read-only worktree — it analyzes but never modifies your code directly.
The simplification cycle
/simplify collects files changed on the feature branch
&darr;
Launches the Code Simplifier agent (Opus, worktree, read-only)
&darr;
Agent analyzes four categories:
Dead code · Abstraction flattening · API simplification · Dependency reduction
&darr;
Presents suggestions one at a time for your approval
&darr;
Each accepted change is applied and tests re-run
If tests fail → automatic revert
Suggestions are categorized by impact (high, medium, low) and include before/after snippets, estimated line reduction, and confidence ratings. You approve or reject each individually. Reports are saved to .vibecrew/simplifications/.
The analysis agent cannot write files. Only the /simplify skill applies approved changes in the main session, and every change is verified by running your test suite. Failed tests trigger an automatic revert.
Auto-Healing CI (/heal)
When CI fails, run /heal instead of manually debugging logs. The CI Healer fetches the failure logs from GitHub Actions or GitLab CI pipelines, diagnoses the root cause, and applies targeted fixes — up to 3 attempts.
How it works
Fetch and diagnose
/heal runs gh run view --log-failed (GitHub) or glab ci view (GitLab) to retrieve the CI output, then pattern-matches errors to categorize the failure: build, test, lint, dependency, or environment.
Checkpoint
Before any fix, a git checkpoint is created so all changes can be reverted cleanly if the fix doesn't work.
Fix loop (max 3 attempts)
The CI Healer agent applies the minimum viable fix for the diagnosed failure, then pushes and waits for CI. If CI fails again, it re-diagnoses with the new context and tries a different approach.
Report
A heal report is saved to .vibecrew/ci-heals/ documenting each attempt, diagnosis, fix, and outcome. If all 3 attempts fail, the healer escalates to you with a summary of what it tried.
Failure CategoryCommon PatternsFix Strategy
BuildTypeScript errors, missing imports, syntax errorsFix the type error or import at its source
TestAssertion failures, snapshot mismatches, timeoutsUpdate assertion/snapshot or fix the logic bug
LintESLint/Prettier violationsAuto-fix with the project's lint command
DependencyMissing packages, version conflictsInstall missing dep or resolve version conflict
EnvironmentMissing env vars, wrong Node version, permission errorsUpdate CI config (YAML/TOML) to match requirements
Issue Tracker Integration (/fix-issue)
Connect GitHub Issues or GitLab Issues directly to VibeCrew&rsquo;s development pipeline. Someone files a bug, a human labels it for auto-fix, and VibeCrew diagnoses, implements, tests, and opens a PR or MR — all autonomously. The provider is auto-detected from the git remote URL, with a config override in .vibecrew/config.json.
/fix-issue <number>
Interactive single-issue fix. Fetches the issue from GitHub or GitLab, imports it into the backlog, creates a branch, implements the fix with the Builder agent, runs quality checks, and opens a PR/MR with Fixes #N (or Closes #N on GitLab) for auto-close.
/sync-issues
Batch-import open issues by label (default: autofix) from GitHub or GitLab into the backlog. Zero token cost — pure bash. Then run /run-backlog to process them automatically.
CI Automation
Fully automated CI-triggered fixes. On GitHub, the github-actions-autofix.yml template triggers on issues.labeled events. On GitLab, the gitlab-ci-autofix.yml.template provides equivalent pipeline-triggered fixes. Both run Claude Code CLI headless and comment results back on the issue.
Hotfix vs Full Feature
Bug issues use a hotfix path (Code → Test → Review) that skips planning and design since bugs don&rsquo;t need upfront design work. Issues labeled enhancement or feature-request, or those invoked with --full, use the standard 6-phase Tier 2 cycle.
The import script tracks issue_number on each backlog entry. Running /sync-issues multiple times or calling /fix-issue on an already-imported issue will detect the duplicate and offer to resume instead of creating a new entry.
Opponent Processor (TDR Debate)
Every technology decision deserves a devil's advocate. During Tier 1, after the Stack Scout produces the TDR, VibeCrew automatically invokes the Opponent Processor — a read-only agent that challenges every decision.
What it produces
Counter-arguments
For each technology decision, the opponent generates 2&ndash;3 reasons why the choice might be wrong, citing real-world failure modes and edge cases.
Debate matrix
A structured comparison table scoring each option across 6 criteria: performance, DX, ecosystem, scalability, learning curve, and lock-in risk.
Risk assessment
Identifies the highest-risk decisions and recommends which ones deserve extra scrutiny or prototyping before committing.
After reviewing both the TDR and the counter-analysis, you choose: keep the original decisions, reconsider specific choices, or skip the review. The opponent's analysis is saved alongside the TDR for future reference.
The Stack Scout is optimized to find the best answer quickly. The Opponent Processor is optimized to find where that answer might break. Together, they produce more robust technology decisions than either could alone. This is especially valuable for decisions that are expensive to reverse (database choice, state management, auth provider).
Inter-Feature Context Hygiene (/run-backlog)
When /run-backlog processes multiple features autonomously, stale conversation history from earlier features can degrade quality for later features. VibeCrew solves this with fresh-session Agent delegation.
Primary approach: Each feature's build phases (Plan→Test) are spawned as an Agent tool call with a completely fresh 200k context window. The prepare-feature-context.sh script assembles the feature spec, TDR, architecture diagrams, design system, CLAUDE.md, user profile, and codebase analysis docs into a structured prompt. The Agent runs in its own worktree, eliminating context rot entirely.
Fallback: If Agent delegation is unavailable, VibeCrew falls back to inline execution with /compact between features. This compresses stale history and fires compact-reinject.sh to re-inject fresh project state and architecture diagrams.
With fresh-session execution, feature 10 gets the exact same 200k context quality as feature 1. The orchestrating session only accumulates lightweight state management overhead. This is a significant improvement over compaction, which still carries summarized prior context. See Runtime State for the full technical flow.
Wave-Based Milestones (Complex Features)
Complex features with milestones can now declare dependencies between milestones via the depends_on field. Independent milestones are grouped into waves and executed in parallel.
Dependency Analysis
During the Plan phase, the Builder analyzes shared files and data flow between milestones to populate depends_on. Milestones sharing files or where one produces data another consumes must have explicit dependencies.
Wave Computation
compute-milestone-waves.sh performs topological sort to group milestones into waves. Wave 1 milestones have no dependencies and can run in parallel. Wave 2 depends on Wave 1, etc.
Parallel Execution
Independent milestones in a wave spawn parallel Agent calls, each with its own worktree and fresh context. After a wave completes, merge-milestone-branches.sh merges the results.
Safety Fallbacks
Cycle detection falls back to sequential. Merge conflicts are resolved by file ownership from estimated_files. If all milestones are linear, behavior is unchanged from sequential processing.
Structured Task Plans
Implementation plans now include a structured ## Tasks section alongside the existing free-form sections (Approach, Files, Component Strategy, etc.). Each task has explicit fields:
### Task 1: Create database schema
- Files: `prisma/schema.prisma` (modify)
- Action: Add User and Session models with email, password_hash, created_at
- Verify: `npx prisma validate`
- Done when: Schema validates without errors and includes both models
The Code phase extracts structured tasks via extract-plan-tasks.sh and processes them sequentially: implement the Action, run the Verify command, check the Done criteria, commit per task. Legacy plans without structured tasks fall back to free-form execution. Task count scales with complexity: 2-3 for trivial, 4-6 for standard, 6-8 per milestone for complex.
Plan Freshness Checks
When multiple features execute sequentially (especially during /run-backlog), earlier features may modify files that later features planned against. VibeCrew records the git SHA when each plan completes and checks for drift before the Code phase starts.
How it works:
Plan phase completes → git SHA recorded in state.json
Code phase starts → check-plan-staleness.sh diffs plan files against recorded SHA
Severity determines response: proceed, review, or refresh affected tasks
Severity levels:
Minor (1&ndash;2 files, <20 lines): Re-read affected files, proceed
Major (3+ files or >50 lines): Refresh affected plan tasks
Critical (deleted/renamed files): Mandatory re-plan of affected tasks
Behavior adapts to your autonomy setting — full_auto refreshes silently, collaborative asks before refreshing, supervised shows full diffs.
Persistent Codebase Analysis
When you onboard an existing project with /onboard, VibeCrew generates 4 persistent analysis documents in .vibecrew/analysis/ that capture your codebase's stack, architecture, conventions, and gaps. These docs are auto-injected into every Plan phase and post-compaction context, eliminating the need to re-discover conventions each session.
stack.md
Language, framework, runtime, package manager, key dependencies, component library, database, deployment target.
architecture.md
Source directories, component organization, API routes, schema location, state management, error handling, auth approach.
conventions.md
Code style (quotes, semicolons, indent), formatter/linter, naming patterns, import style, commit format, test framework.
gaps.md
Source vs test file count, estimated coverage, untested modules (top 10), deprecated dependencies, TODO count.
Analysis docs are committed to git (not gitignored) and persist across sessions and team members. Staleness detection runs on session startup — if docs are >30 days old with >50 commits, or package.json changed, VibeCrew warns you. Refresh with /onboard --refresh (re-runs the auditor without re-generating CLAUDE.md or re-initializing state).
Cost & Safety
Cost Tracking & Safety
VibeCrew provides real-time cost visibility and multi-layered safety enforcement. Cost tracking runs at zero token cost via hook scripts, and safety hooks block destructive operations before they execute.
Cost Dashboard (/cost)
Run /cost at any time to see a complete financial picture of your AI usage.
Current Session
Live cost, turn count, model name, and last-updated timestamp. Read from .vibecrew/session-cost.json which is updated after every assistant turn.
Aggregates
Daily, weekly, monthly, and all-time totals calculated by aggregate-costs.sh from session log files in .vibecrew/sessions/.
Threshold Status
Visual progress bars showing proximity to session warning, session max, and daily warning limits. Configurable in .vibecrew/config.json.
Pricing Reference
Per-model pricing table for Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku showing input, cache write, cache read, and output costs per million tokens.
Model pricing (per million tokens)
ModelInputCache WriteCache ReadOutput
Opus$15.00$18.75$1.50$75.00
Sonnet$3.00$3.75$0.30$15.00
Haiku$0.25$0.30$0.03$1.25
Cost Guardrails
The cost-guardrails.sh hook runs on every Stop event, calculating per-turn costs with model-aware pricing and accumulating totals in .vibecrew/session-cost.json. Alongside cost monitoring, the Stop hook also runs quality-gate.sh, which detects modified source files and runs typecheck/lint/build checks automatically. See Hooks for details.
ThresholdDefaultConfig KeyAction
Session Warning
$2.00
cost_limits.session_warn_usd
Emits a cost warning to the agent
Session Hard Limit
$5.00
cost_limits.session_max_usd
Agent MUST pause and ask for permission to continue
Daily Warning
$20.00
cost_limits.daily_warn_usd
Emits a daily spend warning
Daily totals are calculated by summing estimated_cost_usd from all session files matching today&rsquo;s date, plus the live session cost. All thresholds are configurable in .vibecrew/config.json.
Safety Hooks
VibeCrew enforces safety through PreToolUse hooks (protect-data.sh, phase-gate.sh, restrict-paths.sh) and permission rules in settings.json. These block destructive commands, enforce foundation-before-code ordering, and restrict file writes to the project directory — all at zero token cost.
See the Permissions & Safety page for the full breakdown of hooks, permission rules, and enforcement layers.
Both /heal and /new-feature create a git checkpoint (vibecrew-checkpoint-<timestamp>) before making changes. If anything goes wrong, /undo can roll back to any checkpoint. Checkpoints are lightweight git tags that don&rsquo;t add repository overhead.
Security Audit (/audit)
Run /audit to perform an OWASP Top 10 security analysis of your project. The Security Auditor agent operates in a read-only worktree — it analyzes your code but never modifies it.
What it checks
Injection vulnerabilities — SQL injection, command injection, XSS
Authentication & authorization — missing auth checks, insecure session handling
Secrets exposure — hardcoded API keys, tokens, credentials in source
Dependency vulnerabilities — runs language-specific audit tools (npm audit, pip audit, etc.)
Security headers & configuration — missing CORS, CSP, HSTS headers
Findings are categorized by severity (critical, high, medium, low) and saved to .vibecrew/. The audit adapts to your project's language — see Multi-Language Support for details.
More Commands
These commands cover specialized workflows. Each is a single slash command that orchestrates the right agent(s) and scripts.
/handoff
Generates a structured context transfer document capturing in-progress work, decisions made, and next steps. Use when context is running low or you need to continue in a new session.
/pause
Checkpoints the active feature: commits WIP changes, creates a pause handoff file, cleans up the worktree, and preserves the branch. Use when you need to switch context mid-feature.
/resume
Resumes a previously paused feature: restores state, recreates the worktree from the preserved branch, and continues at the paused phase. Session Startup auto-detects paused features.
/release
Automates version bumps, changelog generation from conventional commits, and release notes creation. The Doc Generator compiles a release summary from git history and session logs.
/tdd
Test-driven development workflow: write a failing test first, then implement until it passes, then refactor. The Verifier agent guides the red-green-refactor cycle.
/debug
Structured debugging with hypothesis testing. The Builder agent systematically isolates the issue, forms hypotheses, tests each one, and applies the fix.
/e2e
Generates Playwright end-to-end tests using the Page Object Model pattern. Tests cover user flows defined in the feature spec and run in real browsers.
/perf-test
Generates k6 performance test suites covering load, stress, spike, and soak scenarios. Establishes baselines for response times and throughput.
/a11y
Runs WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility scanning via axe-core. Reports violations by severity with fix suggestions. Contributes +2 to Vibe Score when clean.
Language Support
Multi-Language Support
While VibeCrew was designed with JavaScript/TypeScript projects in mind, it supports 7 languages for onboarding, convention detection, security auditing, and dependency scanning.

How language detection works
detect-conventions.sh scans project root for manifests
&darr;
Identifies language from: package.json, pyproject.toml, Gemfile, go.mod, Cargo.toml, composer.json, pom.xml
&darr;
extract-project-conventions.sh detects per-language:
framework, ORM, auth library, API patterns, naming conventions
&darr;
Results feed into Code Auditor and CLAUDE.md generation
Where language support applies
/onboard — Code Auditor detects language, conventions, frameworks, and test gaps for all 7 languages
/audit — Security Auditor runs language-specific dependency audit tools and adapts OWASP scanning patterns
PostToolUse formatting — format-code.sh auto-formats with the correct tool: Prettier (JS/TS), Black (Python), rustfmt (Rust), gofmt (Go)
/new-project — Stack Scout research adapts to the detected or chosen language ecosystem
Node.js/TypeScript projects receive &ldquo;high&rdquo; confidence from the Code Auditor due to deeper ecosystem integration. Other languages receive &ldquo;medium&rdquo; confidence — the core workflow (Tier 1 foundation, Tier 2 cycle, Vibe Score, hooks) works identically, but framework-specific patterns may need manual refinement in CLAUDE.md.
Parallel Backlog Execution
/run-backlog --parallel enables wave-based parallel processing of independent features.
The system analyzes feature dependencies via analyze-feature-dependencies.sh and groups
features into waves where no feature depends on another within the same wave.
AspectSequential (default)Parallel (--parallel)
ExecutionOne feature at a timeUp to N features per wave (default: 3)
DependenciesPriority orderWave-based: independent features grouped together
Quality gatePer featurePer wave (after merge)
Cost guardrailsPer featureMultiplied by concurrent agents per wave
Merge strategySequential on mainSequential merge between waves
How it works under the hood
Parallel features are not separate Claude Code sessions or terminal tabs. Each feature
runs as a concurrent Agent tool call within the same parent orchestration session.
Every Agent call gets its own fresh 200k context window and isolated git worktree — so
features cannot interfere with each other&apos;s files or accumulate stale context.
The parent session stays lightweight: it manages wave ordering, monitors Agent completion,
runs the quality gate after each wave merges, and advances to the next wave. The
analyze-feature-dependencies.sh script performs a topological sort on the
depends_on fields to compute which features can safely run in the same wave.
Use --parallel when your backlog has 3+ features with few dependencies between them.
For backlogs with chain dependencies (A→B→C), parallel mode adds no benefit and falls back to sequential.
Agent Overlay System
Customize any agent&apos;s behavior per-project by creating override files in
.vibecrew/agent-overrides/<agent>.md. Override sections with matching
## Heading names replace the base section; new headings are appended. YAML
frontmatter (model, tools, isolation) is always preserved from the base agent.
Overrides survive plugin updates because they live in your project, not the plugin.
See the Personalization page for details.

## How It Works

How VibeCrew Works
VibeCrew is a system of interlocking parts: a plugin shell, specialized agents, lifecycle hooks, slash commands, bash scripts, and per-project runtime state. Each piece solves a specific problem that emerges when AI builds software autonomously.
Seven Problems VibeCrew Solves
Rule Drift
Context Bloat
Session Amnesia
Workflow Errors
Quality Decay
Ad-Hoc Decisions
Split Attention
Problem
AI forgets rules mid-session
Large language models don't reliably follow instructions embedded in long contexts. The more code and conversation accumulates, the more likely the model is to ignore project conventions, skip required steps, or write code before the architecture is decided.
How VibeCrew solves this
Phase gate hookA bash script intercepts every file write. If foundation artifacts (VISION.md, TDR, architecture diagrams) aren't complete, the write is blocked before the model even sees the result.
Quality gate hookAfter every task completion, typecheck, lint, and build run automatically. Failures are caught instantly, not deferred to a later review.
Path restriction hookWrites outside the project root are blocked, preventing accidental modifications to system files or other projects.
Zero token costAll enforcement runs as bash scripts in lifecycle hooks. No tokens are spent reminding the model of rules — they're enforced deterministically.
View hook system →
Problem
Context windows fill up fast
Research tasks — reading documentation, evaluating libraries, analyzing codebases — consume thousands of tokens. Once the context window fills, the model loses earlier instructions and code, forcing expensive restarts.
How VibeCrew solves this
Worktree isolationExpensive agents (Stack Scout, Builder, Code Reviewer) run in separate git worktrees with their own context windows. Only their distilled output re-enters the main session.
MCP serversContext7 serves library documentation on demand. Chrome DevTools inspects live pages. No need to paste large blocks of reference material.
Fresh-session executionDuring /run-backlog, each feature is spawned as an isolated Agent tool call with a clean 200k context window. Context rot is eliminated entirely — no compaction needed. Falls back to inline execution with /compact between features if Agent delegation is unavailable.
Context warningsA Stop hook monitors usage and warns at 45% and 60%, giving you time to wrap up before hitting the limit.
View agent topology →
Problem
No persistent memory across sessions
Each Claude Code session starts with a blank slate. Without external state, the AI can't know which features are done, what phase you're in, what decisions were made, or what quality trends look like over time.
How VibeCrew solves this
.vibecrew/state.jsonTracks foundation completion status, the active feature, and current phase. Every session starts by reading this file to resume exactly where you left off.
Backlog & signalsFeature specs live in backlog.json. Inter-agent signals coordinate handoffs between agents working in parallel.
Session logs & scoresEvery session is logged with its Vibe Score breakdown. The Performance Coach reads score history to detect patterns across multiple sessions.
Handoff documentsWhen context runs low, /handoff generates a structured document capturing all in-progress work, decisions, and next steps for the next session.
Persistent analysis docsFor brownfield projects, /onboard generates four persistent markdown files in .vibecrew/analysis/ (stack, architecture, conventions, gaps). These are auto-injected into Plan phases and post-compaction context, so agents never need to rediscover project conventions from scratch.
View state structure →
Problem
Manual workflows are error-prone
Remembering to run tests, update docs, check accessibility, format code, and write a changelog entry after every feature is tedious. Steps get skipped, especially during long sessions or when working under pressure.
How VibeCrew solves this
Slash commands/wrap runs quality checks, generates docs, updates the changelog, computes the Vibe Score, and commits — in a single trigger.
/run-backlogPlans, builds, tests, reviews, and documents every feature in the backlog sequentially, with automatic compaction between features.
Auto-formatting hookEvery file write triggers Prettier/formatter automatically. Code style is never a manual step.
Slash commandsCover the full lifecycle — from /setup and /plan-features through /tdd, /review, /e2e, /a11y, to /release.
View command reference →
Problem
Quality degrades without oversight
AI-generated code tends to accumulate dead code, unnecessary abstractions, and subtle regressions over time. Without continuous feedback, each session makes the codebase slightly worse — and nobody notices until it's a mess.
How VibeCrew solves this
Vibe ScoreA quantitative quality metric computed every session. Starts at 100, applies deductions for prompt churn, tool loops, missing tests, skipped reviews, and documentation drift. Bonuses for TDD, clean sessions, and full coverage.
Performance CoachAnalyzes score trends across sessions. When anti-patterns recur 3+ times, it proposes permanent CLAUDE.md rule mutations — creating a self-improving feedback loop.
Code ReviewerRead-only review against the feature spec, TDR compliance, and project conventions. Catches architectural drift before it ships.
Code SimplifierDetects dead code, flattens unnecessary abstractions, and reduces API surface area. Runs on demand via /simplify.
View feedback loop →
Problem
Architecture decisions are ad-hoc
Without a structured research phase, AI picks whatever framework or pattern it saw most in training data. Technology choices are made implicitly during coding rather than explicitly during planning — leading to inconsistent stacks and regretted decisions.
How VibeCrew solves this
Two-tier workflowTier 1 (foundation) must complete before any source code is written. This includes VISION.md, design system, TDR, and architecture diagrams — enforced by the phase gate hook.
Stack Scout agentA dedicated research agent that evaluates technologies in an isolated worktree, produces a structured Technology Decision Record (TDR), and never writes application code.
Opponent ProcessorA devil's advocate agent that stress-tests TDR decisions with debate matrices and risk assessments before development begins.
Architecture diagramsFive Mermaid diagrams (system topology, schema, state flows, API sequences, component tree) are generated during Tier 1 and referenced by every agent.
View two-tier workflow →
Problem
You have to babysit every session
Without automation, you're glued to the terminal — reading every output, deciding when to intervene, and context-switching constantly. Running multiple projects in parallel is impossible because each session demands your continuous attention.
How VibeCrew solves this
Interrupt-only notificationsThe system stays silent during normal operation and only pings you on three conditions: permission stalls, task completion, and critical failures. No noise, no polling.
Warp deep-linkingNotifications include warp://session/<id> URIs that jump you straight to the terminal tab that needs attention — no hunting through tabs.
Autonomous feature builds/run-backlog processes the entire feature queue autonomously — planning, building, testing, reviewing, and documenting each feature without manual triggers between steps.
Multi-project parallel workCombined with per-project state (.vibecrew/), you can run VibeCrew across several projects simultaneously, responding only when notified.
View Warp integration →

## Bash Scripts

Bash Scripts
Scripts are the worker bees of VibeCrew — small bash programs that do the actual mechanical work. While agents think and make decisions, scripts create files, update project state, calculate scores, and send notifications. They run in milliseconds and always produce the same result for the same input.
&#9632;
What they are
Deterministic bash scripts organized by function: core lifecycle, feature management, quality scoring, project analysis, documentation, gamification, and state management. Agents never write state files directly — all mutations go through scripts.
&#10003;
What problem they solve
AI token cost scales with complexity. By offloading mechanical tasks (JSON manipulation, git operations, file formatting) to scripts, VibeCrew keeps AI focused on decisions while scripts handle bookkeeping at zero token cost. Scripts also guarantee consistency — state mutations are atomic and predictable.
Core Lifecycle
Scripts that run during session startup and completion.
ScriptCalled ByWhat It Does
session-startup.shHookEnvironment check, terminal detection, state loading, and workflow routing on every session start.
quality-gate.shHookRuns typecheck, lint, and build on modified files at task completion. Blocks on failure.
statusline.shHookUpdates the terminal status bar with current feature, phase, and Vibe Score.
notify.shHookSends native OS notifications for permission stalls, completions, and errors.
Feature Management
Scripts that manage the feature lifecycle and backlog.
ScriptCalled ByWhat It Does
update-backlog.shAgent / SkillAdds, updates, or moves features in backlog.json. Manages Kanban column transitions.
complete-phase.shAgent / SkillMarks a development phase as done and advances to the next phase in the 6-phase cycle.
git-branch-create.shAgentCreates a feature branch with consistent naming: feat/<feature-name>.
create-checkpoint.shAgentCreates a git tag checkpoint before risky operations so you can roll back with /undo.
Quality & Scoring
Scripts that calculate Vibe Scores and analyze quality.
ScriptCalled ByWhat It Does
calculate-vibe-score.shAgentComputes the session's Vibe Score (0&ndash;130) based on deductions and bonuses across quality dimensions.
aggregate-scores.shAgentAggregates Vibe Scores across sessions for trend analysis and Performance Coach input.
analyze-test-gaps.shAgentCompares modified source files against test coverage to identify untested code paths.
apply-mutation.shAgentApplies Performance Coach CLAUDE.md mutation proposals after user approval.
Project Analysis
Scripts that analyze the codebase and extract patterns.
ScriptCalled ByWhat It Does
detect-conventions.shAgentScans the codebase for naming conventions, file patterns, and code style to populate CLAUDE.md.
extract-design-system.shAgentExtracts CSS tokens, color palette, typography, and spacing from existing stylesheets.
detect-secrets.shAgentScans for accidentally committed secrets, API keys, and credentials.
scan-dependencies.shAgentAudits dependencies for known vulnerabilities and license compliance issues.
State & Config
Scripts that manage the .vibecrew/ runtime state.
ScriptCalled ByWhat It Does
init-vibecrew-state.shSkillCreates the initial .vibecrew/ directory structure and default JSON files during /setup.
migrate-state.shSkillMigrates state files between VibeCrew versions when schemas change.
generate-handoff.shSkillCreates a structured context transfer document for cross-session continuity.
detect-terminal.shSkillDetects terminal type (Warp, iTerm2, VS Code, etc.) and configures notification and deep-link support.
Agent Infrastructure
Scripts that manage agent identity, memory, expertise, and per-project overrides.
ScriptCalled ByWhat It Does

Documentation & Release

drift-tracker.shAgentCompares modified source files against existing docs to detect documentation drift.
Gamification & Progression

Progression & Rewards
Gamification System
VibeCrew includes a persistent progression layer that motivates across sessions and teaches vibe-coding skills over time. It tracks your growth from your first /setup through hundreds of shipped features.
&#9878;
Artifacts over actions
Rewards map to real outputs — shipped features, passing tests, clean sessions — not arbitrary clicks.
&#9733;
Teaching over tracking
Every mechanic helps you improve. Challenges target your weakest skills. Quizzes explain the answer.
&#9829;
Sustainable over addictive
Grace periods for streaks, opt-in challenges, no toxic leaderboards. Taking time off is never punished.
The gamification pipeline runs automatically at the end of every /wrap. Six scripts execute sequentially: award XP, check level-up, update streak, distribute skill XP, check badges, and update challenges. You never need to run anything manually.
Configuration
Enabling & Disabling
There are two ways to control gamification, and they stay in sync automatically.
Option 1: User Profile (recommended)
Run /profile and answer the gamification question. This sets the gamification_preference dimension, and VibeCrew automatically syncs the corresponding config flags.
Profile SettingWhat You SeeConfig Flags
All In (full)
XP, badges, streaks, challenges, level-ups, streak reminders, quizzes — everything
enabled: true, show_xp: true, streak_reminders: true
Light Touch (light)
XP and badges display, but no streak reminders — low-key progression
enabled: true, show_xp: true, streak_reminders: false
Score Only (score_only)
Vibe Score only. No XP, no badges, no streaks display. Progression still tracked silently
enabled: true, show_xp: false, streak_reminders: false
Disabled (disabled)
All gamification output suppressed. Vibe Score and Performance Coach still operate independently
enabled: false, show_xp: false, streak_reminders: false
Option 2: Direct config edit
Edit .vibecrew/config.json directly. The gamification block controls everything:
Full gamification (all features on)
Gamification disabled
All gamification scripts check config.json on entry. When enabled is false, every script exits immediately with no output and no file modifications. Your gamification.json data is preserved — nothing is deleted. Re-enable at any time and pick up where you left off.
Disabling gamification does not disable the Vibe Score. The score measures session quality and feeds the Performance Coach — it operates as a core system, not a gamification feature. You always get your score at /wrap.
Session Quality
Vibe Score
Every session ends with a quality score (0&ndash;130+). It starts at 100 and adjusts based on real work artifacts. The score is the single data source for XP, badges, challenges, and Performance Coach analysis.
Deductions
Points are removed for anti-patterns detected during the session:
Anti-PatternDeductionWhat It Means
Prompt churn&minus;5 per sequenceRephrasing the same instruction multiple times without progress
Tool loops&minus;10 per loopRetrying the same failed command with the same approach
Low cache utilization&minus;15Cache ratio below 50% (inefficient token usage)
Context violations&minus;20Peak context usage exceeded 60% of the window
No tests&minus;10Test files exist but zero tests pass
No feature spec&minus;5Active feature missing acceptance criteria
Skipped code review&minus;5Review phase not completed for the feature
Documentation drift&minus;3 per stale docSource code changed but matching feature docs not updated
Console errors&minus;5Console errors detected on affected pages
Visual token violations&minus;3 each (max &minus;9)Design system token violations (hardcoded colors, wrong spacing, etc.)
Plan revisions &ge; 2&minus;5Plan or spec revised 2+ times mid-feature (insufficient upfront planning)
Expected artifacts per phase: Plan → docs/features/&lbrace;name&rbrace;/plan.md, Design → design.md, Code → source files, Test → test files, Docs → feature documentation. Trivial features skip Design and Review, so missing design.md or review reports are not penalized for trivial complexity.
Bonuses
Points are awarded for best practices:
Best PracticeBonusCondition
Complete phase artifacts+30 maxAll Tier 2 phases (Plan, UI, Code, Test, Review, Docs) completed
High cache utilization+10Cache ratio above 70%
Full test coverage+15Coverage above 80%
Clean session+5Zero deductions
TDD discipline+3Tests written before implementation code
E2E tests passing+3Playwright/E2E suite passes
Accessibility clean+2No critical or serious a11y issues
Code review complete+2Review phase completed for the feature
Performance baselines+2Performance metrics tracked
Visual compliance clean+3Design system tokens used correctly throughout
A session with zero deductions and all bonuses can score 130+. This is rare but achievable — it means you planned thoroughly, wrote tests first, hit high cache, shipped with docs, and kept the context window lean.
Progression
XP & Leveling
XP is earned through real development work. Every source maps to existing tracked data — there are no gamification-only actions to grind.

Leveling curve
XP per level follows an exponential curve: floor(100 &times; 1.15(level&minus;1)). Early levels come quickly to build momentum. Later levels require sustained consistent work.

Consistency
Streaks
Streaks track consecutive days of coding. They&rsquo;re designed to celebrate consistency without demanding it — a broken streak is just a number, not a loss.
How they work
&#128197;
Increments on /wrap
Each calendar day you run /wrap counts. Multiple wraps per day still count as one.
&#127774;
Weekend auto-grace
Saturdays and Sundays never break streaks and never consume grace credits. Take weekends off freely.
&#10052;
2 grace days per month
Miss a weekday? The streak continues if you have grace days remaining. Resets on the 1st of each month.
&#128154;
No penalty for breaking
When a streak breaks, the counter resets to 0. No XP is lost, no badges are revoked. Start fresh.
&#128276;
Reminders are opt-in
Streak reminders are disabled by default. Enable via /profile (set gamification to &ldquo;All In&rdquo;) or in config.json.
Streak data tracked
FieldWhat It Stores
streak.currentCurrent consecutive day count
streak.longestAll-time longest streak (for bragging rights)
streak.last_session_dateLast date /wrap was run
streak.grace_days_remainingGrace credits left this month (0&ndash;2)
streak.frozen_todayWhether a grace day was used today

Learning
Quizzes
Short (3&ndash;5 question) knowledge checks delivered interactively in the CLI. Each question shows the correct answer and an educational explanation regardless of whether you got it right. Quizzes unlock at Level 3.
Available quizzes
QuizTopicLevelQuestions
context-management-101Cache utilization, Context7, token efficiency35
prompting-basicsClear instructions, reducing churn, spec-first35
testing-disciplineTDD-hybrid, when to test first vs after34
architecture-planningTDR purpose, foundation artifacts, phase gates34
workflow-masteryPhase sequence, /wrap, /check, streaks35
advanced-contextSubagent isolation, compaction, cache optimization154
advanced-testingPlaywright, axe-core, spec-first vs impl-first154
How quizzes are triggered
Explicit: Run /quiz for a random quiz, or /quiz context-management-101 for a specific one
Contextual: The Performance Coach suggests a relevant quiz after /wrap when it detects an anti-pattern (e.g., low cache → context-management-101)
Periodic: Session Startup suggests an overdue quiz if more than 30 days since the last one (never forces it)
XP from quizzes
+5 XP per correct answer, awarded only on first completion. You can retake quizzes for practice but won&rsquo;t earn XP again. Quiz XP is intentionally modest — it cannot substitute for real work XP.
Self-Improvement
Performance Coach
The Performance Coach is an Opus agent that analyzes Vibe Score trends across sessions and proposes permanent improvements to your project&rsquo;s CLAUDE.md. It&rsquo;s the self-improving feedback loop at the heart of VibeCrew.
How it works
1
Detection
Reads the latest score file, extracts deduction patterns
2
Correlation
Cross-references against MEMORY.md to find recurring patterns
3
Eligibility
Validates against guardrails: min 5 sessions, no duplicates, not recently rejected
4
Proposal
Generates a specific CLAUDE.md rule mutation targeting the highest-impact pattern
5
Decision
You approve, reject, or edit the mutation. Rejections have a cooldown period
6
Recording
Updates MEMORY.md and mutation-log.json for future analysis
Guardrails
Max 1 mutation per session — prevents overwhelming changes
Min 5 sessions required before any mutation is proposed
3-rejection cooldown: rejected patterns wait rejection_count &times; 7 days before being proposed again
No duplicate rules — won&rsquo;t propose what already exists in CLAUDE.md
No hook-redundant rules — won&rsquo;t propose rules that hooks already enforce
Max 15 Session Learnings in CLAUDE.md — auto-prunes oldest entries
Pattern templates
The coach tracks six anti-pattern categories and generates targeted mutation proposals:
PatternScore ImpactExample Mutation
Prompt Churn&minus;5 per sequence&ldquo;Write acceptance criteria before starting implementation&rdquo;
Tool Loops&minus;10 per loop&ldquo;After 2 failed attempts, change approach instead of retrying&rdquo;
Low Cache&minus;15&ldquo;Use Context7 for library docs instead of pasting them&rdquo;
Context Violations&minus;20&ldquo;Offload research to worktree subagents&rdquo;
Missing Artifacts&minus;5&ldquo;Always run /check before /wrap&rdquo;
Documentation Drift&minus;3 per doc&ldquo;Update feature docs in the same session as code changes&rdquo;
Visualization
Achievements Dashboard
There are two ways to view your gamification data:
CLI view (/achievements)
A compact text summary showing your level, badges, streak, and active challenges. Available from any terminal session.
Achievements: Level 7 "Focused Builder" | 8/21 badges | Streak: 12 days
Open full dashboard: http://localhost:5173/achievements
Visual dashboard
The VitePress dashboard provides the full visual experience:

Level badge (color-coded by tier), title, XP progress bar, streak counter, total sessions and features shipped.
Badge Gallery
3-column grid with category tabs (Milestones, Skills, Special). Earned badges full-color, locked badges faded with progress.
Skill Radar Chart
SVG 5-axis spider chart showing skill levels. Your development profile shape at a glance.

GitHub-style 12-week heatmap. Color intensity = Vibe Score. Grace days marked with a frost icon.
Active Challenges
Cards for each challenge with progress bar, time remaining, and type badge.
Score Sparkline
Last 30 sessions as a mini SVG line chart with trend arrow and average.
Technical Details
Data Files & Storage
All gamification state is stored locally in your project&rsquo;s .vibecrew/ directory. Nothing leaves your machine.
FilePurposeUpdated By
.vibecrew/gamification.jsonLevel, XP, badges, skills, streaks, challenges, quiz progress, statsaward-xp.sh, check-badges.sh, update-streak.sh, etc.
.vibecrew/config.jsonGamification toggle, streak reminders, quiz frequency, user profile/profile, manual edit
.vibecrew/scores/score-*.jsonPer-session Vibe Score breakdown (deductions, metrics, phases)calculate-vibe-score.sh
MEMORY.mdPerformance Coach persistent memory (anti-patterns, mutations, trends)Performance Coach agent
.vibecrew/mutation-log.jsonHistory of proposed, accepted, and rejected CLAUDE.md mutationsapply-mutation.sh
Concurrency safety
All gamification scripts use advisory locks (.vibecrew/locks/gamification.lock) and atomic writes (temp file + mv) to prevent corruption when multiple agents update simultaneously.
Your gamification.json file is self-contained. If you move to a new machine, copy .vibecrew/gamification.json and .vibecrew/config.json to preserve your full progression history.

## Hooks

Hooks
Hooks are automatic safety checks that run behind the scenes at zero token cost. When an agent tries to write a file or run a command, hooks intercept the action and validate it before it executes. Think of them as security guards at every door — they check permissions instantly using small bash scripts, not AI processing.
&#9632;
What they are
Bash scripts triggered by Claude Code lifecycle events (session start, before/after tool use, session end). They read a JSON payload from stdin and return exit code 0 (allow) or 2 (block).
&#10003;
What problem they solve
AI models can forget rules mid-session. Hooks enforce constraints deterministically — the phase gate blocks source code writes before the foundation is complete, the quality gate catches build errors, and the data protector blocks destructive commands. No token cost, no forgetting.
Session Init Hooks
Run automatically when a new Claude Code session starts.
ScriptEventWhat It Does
session-startup.sh
SessionStart
Checks environment (Git, Node, jq), detects terminal type, loads state, and routes to the right workflow.
sync-state.sh
SessionStart
Reconciles state files on startup — ensures .vibecrew/ JSON is consistent after crashes or manual edits.
error-recovery.sh
SessionStart
Clears stale lock files and repairs corrupted state from previous interrupted sessions.
compact-reinject.sh
SessionStart (compact)
Re-injects essential context (active feature, phase, conventions) after Claude Code's /compact clears the context window.
Pre-Action Guards
Intercept actions before they execute. Return exit code 2 to block.
ScriptEventWhat It Does
phase-gate.sh
PreToolUse (Write/Edit)
Blocks source code writes until the Tier 1 foundation (VISION, TDR, architecture, CLAUDE.md) is complete. Prevents coding before decisions are made.
restrict-paths.sh
PreToolUse (Write/Edit)
Blocks file writes outside the project root directory. Prevents agents from modifying system files or other projects.
protect-data.sh
PreToolUse (Bash)
Blocks destructive shell commands: rm -rf, DROP TABLE, DELETE FROM without WHERE, force push, and privilege escalation.
validate-phase-transition.sh
PreToolUse (Bash)
Enforces phase ordering — ensures foundation steps run in sequence and artifacts are complete before advancing.
validate-signal.sh
PreToolUse (Write/Edit)
Validates inter-agent signal file schemas, enum values, and feature ID cross-references before they're written.
Post-Action Processors
Run after an action completes successfully.
ScriptEventWhat It Does
format-code.sh
PostToolUse (Write/Edit)
Auto-formats files after every write using the project's configured formatter (Prettier, ESLint, etc.).
validate-skill-schema.sh
PostToolUse (Write/Edit)
Validates SKILL.md frontmatter on every skill write. Checks required fields, category values, argument-hint consistency, and fork/agent pairing.
notify.sh
Notification / PostToolUseFailure
Sends native OS notifications for permission stalls, task completions, and errors. Includes Warp Terminal deep-links when available.
drift-tracker.sh
PostToolUse (all)
Classifies tool calls as progress/exploration/neutral. Emits soft warnings when exploration count exceeds phase-dependent thresholds (plan: 40, code: 20). Never blocks.
context-monitor-posttool.sh
PostToolUse (all)
Lightweight context window monitor with debouncing (checks every 5th tool use). Injects warnings via additionalContext at three thresholds: 45% INFO, 60% WARNING, 80% CRITICAL. Complements the Stop-hook check-context.sh for defense in depth.
Session End Checks
Run when a session stops to catch issues before they persist.
ScriptEventWhat It Does
quality-gate.sh
Stop
Runs typecheck, lint, and build on modified source files. Blocks task completion if any check fails — the agent must fix errors before finishing.
claude-md-lint.sh
Stop
Validates CLAUDE.md file size and structure. Keeps it under the recommended line limit to avoid context bloat.
cost-guardrails.sh
Stop
Tracks session and daily API costs against configured thresholds. Warns or blocks when spending exceeds limits.
check-context.sh
Stop
Monitors context window usage and warns at 45% and 60%. Helps prevent sessions from running out of context mid-task.
drift-circuit-breaker.sh
Stop
Checks hard drift thresholds (plan: 60, code: 35). Creates WIP commit and blocker signal when exceeded, prompting the agent to change approach. Fail-open (never blocks stop).

## MCP Servers

MCP Servers
MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers give agents access to external tools and services — documentation lookup, browser automation, database inspection, payment APIs, and more. VibeCrew ships with bundled servers and a registry of additional ones that get activated on demand once the project's architecture is clear.
&#9632;
What they are
Lightweight tool servers that run alongside Claude Code via npx. Each server exposes a set of tools (search docs, run browser, query database) that agents can call during their work. Configured in .mcp.json.
&#10003;
What problem they solve
Without MCP servers, agents would paste entire library docs into the context window (~5,000+ tokens per lookup). Context7 replaces that with a single tool call (~1,500 tokens saved per query). Service-specific servers (Supabase, Stripe) let agents inspect schemas and APIs directly instead of guessing from docs.
On-Demand Integration
VibeCrew doesn't load all MCP servers upfront. Only 3 general-purpose servers are enabled by default. The rest activate after the TDR (Technology Decision Record) is finalized during Tier 1, when VibeCrew knows exactly which technologies the project uses.
&#9654;
How auto-discovery works
After TDR approval, sync-mcp-from-tdr.sh reads the technology decisions, pattern-matches them against the MCP registry, and auto-enables matching servers. If the TDR mentions "Supabase," the Supabase MCP server activates. If it mentions "Stripe," payment tools appear. Servers that need environment variables (API keys) are flagged for setup.
&#9888;
Why wait for architecture?
Loading unused MCP servers wastes tool-discovery tokens and clutters the agent's tool list. Claude Code's Tool Search dynamically loads only relevant tool definitions when 5+ servers are active — but fewer active servers still means faster routing and lower overhead.
Default Servers (Always Enabled)
These 3 servers are useful for any project regardless of tech stack. They're enabled in .mcp.json from the start.
ServerWhat It DoesUsed By
Context7
Up-to-date documentation lookup for libraries and frameworks. Replaces pasting docs into context (~1,500 tokens saved per query).
Stack Scout, Builder, all research tasks
Chrome DevTools
Browser automation and inspection via Chrome DevTools Protocol. Navigate pages, inspect elements, capture screenshots.
Builder (visual verification), E2E testing
Playwright
End-to-end browser testing and automation. Drives real browsers for integration tests.
/e2e, Builder (component testing)
Conditional Servers (TDR-Activated)
These 6 servers ship in .mcp.json but start disabled. They activate automatically when the TDR selects matching technologies, or manually via bash scripts/enable-mcp-server.sh <name> enable.
ServerWhat It DoesRequiresTDR Trigger
Semgrep
Static analysis and code security scanning
—
Any project (security audit)
Sentry
Error tracking and performance monitoring
SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN
TDR mentions "sentry"
Supabase
PostgreSQL, auth, storage, real-time subscriptions
SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY
TDR mentions "supabase"
Stripe
Payment processing, subscriptions, invoicing
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY
TDR mentions "stripe" or "payments"
Vercel
Deployment, serverless functions, edge config
VERCEL_TOKEN
TDR mentions "vercel"
Figma
Design file access and design-to-code workflows
FIGMA_ACCESS_TOKEN
TDR mentions "figma"
Extended Registry
Beyond the bundled servers, templates/mcp-registry.json contains additional servers that can be auto-discovered from TDR technology choices. When a match is found, VibeCrew recommends the server and provides setup instructions.
Database & ORM
ServerWhat It DoesRequires
FirebaseFirestore, auth, hosting, cloud functions—
PrismaType-safe ORM for PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite—
MongoDBDocument database with Atlas cloud and Mongoose ODMMDB_MCP_CONNECTION_STRING
NeonServerless PostgreSQL with branching and autoscalingNEON_API_KEY
Upstash RedisServerless Redis and Kafka for caching and messagingUPSTASH_EMAIL, UPSTASH_API_KEY
Authentication
ServerWhat It DoesRequires
ClerkAuthentication and user management with prebuilt UICLERK_SECRET_KEY
Auth0Identity platform with SSO, MFA, social login—
Hosting, Frameworks & Infrastructure
ServerWhat It DoesRequires
NetlifyWeb hosting, serverless functions, edge deployment—
RailwayInfrastructure platform for deploying apps and databases—
ShopifyE-commerce platform and Hydrogen framework—
Next.js DevToolsNext.js development tools and route inspection—
shadcn/uiComponent library with Tailwind CSS and Radix UI—
TerraformInfrastructure as Code for cloud provisioning—
KubernetesContainer orchestration and cluster management—
ResendEmail API for transactional and marketing emailsRESEND_API_KEY
Fallback & Health Monitoring
All MCP servers are optional. If a server fails to connect, crashes, or isn't configured, agents gracefully fall back to built-in tools. No MCP server is required for VibeCrew to function.
&#10003;
Graceful degradation
If the Supabase MCP is unavailable, the Builder reads migration files instead of inspecting the live schema. If Context7 is down, agents use WebSearch. Every agent's prompt includes explicit fallback instructions.
&#9888;
Health probes
check-mcp-health.sh sends a JSON-RPC initialize probe to each enabled server with a 2-second timeout. Failed servers are reported as "degraded" in /status output.

---

## Companion Skills

Companion Skills
Companion skills are third-party Claude Code skills that extend VibeCrew with specialized domain expertise — frontend aesthetics, framework best practices, database optimization, security analysis, and more. VibeCrew automatically recommends relevant skills after your TDR is approved, following the same pattern-matching approach as MCP server sync.
&#9632;
What they are
SKILL.md files published by official vendors (Anthropic, Vercel, Supabase, Cloudflare, Stripe) that inject domain-specific rules and patterns into Claude Code sessions. Unlike MCP servers (which provide tool access), skills provide knowledge and conventions — best practices, optimization rules, and design guidelines.
&#10003;
What problem they solve
VibeCrew handles architecture, workflow orchestration, and code quality. But domain-specific expertise (React re-render optimization, Postgres query tuning, Core Web Vitals auditing) is better maintained by the technology vendors themselves. Companion skills bring that vendor expertise into VibeCrew sessions without bloating agent prompts.
Three Ways to Get Skills
&#9654;
1. Auto-recommend (Registry)
After TDR approval, recommend-companion-skills.sh pattern-matches your technology choices against the curated registry (templates/companion-skills.json). If your TDR mentions "React" and "Supabase," it recommends React Best Practices, Web Design Guidelines, Frontend Design, and Supabase Postgres Best Practices.
&#9888;
2. Discovery (skills.sh)
For TDR technologies with no registry match (e.g., Prisma, Drizzle), VibeCrew searches the broader ecosystem in priority order: Anthropic skills → official vendor repos → skills.sh. Every discovered skill passes through a 5-gate quality check before being recommended.
&#10003;
3. Manual (/install-skill)
Install any skill directly — GitHub repos, local paths, or company-internal repositories. Run /install-skill https://github.com/my-company/our-skills or /install-skill /path/to/local/skill. Safety validation runs automatically for remote sources.
5-Gate Quality Check
Every discovered skill (from skills.sh or manual install of remote sources) passes through validate-skill-safety.sh before being recommended or installed. All 5 gates must pass.
GateCheckReject If
1. Trusted Author
Compare GitHub org against allowlist (Anthropic, Vercel, Cloudflare, Supabase, Stripe, Trail of Bits, Clerk, Hookdeck, Netlify, Prisma)
Unknown org gets a warning flag (shown to user, not auto-rejected)
2. Repo Health
GitHub API: stars, last commit date, license
<20 stars OR no commits in 6 months OR no license
3. SKILL.md Scan
Read SKILL.md content, check size and structure
>15KB (bloated) or missing expected structure
4. Dangerous Patterns
Grep for: rm -rf, curl|sh, eval, exec(, process.env reads of secrets, base64 decode, outbound fetch
Any match = reject
5. Script Audit
If skill has scripts/ directory, scan each file
Network calls to non-GitHub URLs, file deletion outside project, env var exfiltration
Skills from trusted authors with a passing verdict are recommended directly. Skills from unknown authors with a passing verdict are recommended with a warning: "This skill is from an unverified author. Review it before installing."
Curated Registry
The registry at templates/companion-skills.json contains pre-vetted skills from official vendors. These are always safe to recommend — no quality gate needed.
SkillAuthorCategoryWhat It DoesTDR Triggers
Frontend Design
Anthropic
