Distinctive, production-grade frontend aesthetics — anti-AI-slop typography, color, and motion
Any frontend framework, Tailwind, CSS

How VibeCrew Adapts
When companion skills are detected, VibeCrew agents adjust their behavior to avoid duplication and leverage the skill's expertise.
&#9654;
Builder + Frontend Design
When Anthropic's frontend-design skill is installed, the Builder defers typography, color aesthetic, and motion choices to the skill. Design specs focus on component architecture, data flow, and business patterns instead. Wireframes remain unchanged (they're about layout, not aesthetics).
&#9632;
Detection mechanism
detect-companion-skill.sh checks ~/.claude/skills/ and .claude/skills/ for installed skill folders. Agents call this lightweight script inline before phases where skill overlap would occur.
Manual Installation
Use /install-skill to add any skill — including company-internal, private, or custom skills that aren't in the registry or on skills.sh.
Examples
CommandSource TypeQuality Gate
/install-skill vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill react-best-practices
GitHub (public)
Full validation
/install-skill https://github.com/my-company/internal-skills
GitHub (private)
Full validation (requires gh auth)
/install-skill /path/to/local/skill
Local path (in project)
Skipped (trusted)
/install-skill ~/company-skills/our-patterns
Local path (outside project)
Full validation
Installed skills are tracked in .vibecrew/config.json under companion_skills.manual with source, install timestamp, and safety verdict.
Companion Skills vs MCP Servers
Both extend VibeCrew, but they serve different purposes.

Notes
&#9888;
No official backend skill
As of March 2026, no official vendor publishes a general backend development skill. VibeCrew's Tier 2 workflow (Builder agent, TDR boundaries, Context7 docs) covers backend development natively.
&#9632;
Trail of Bits for security
Trail of Bits (trailofbits/skills) offers 40+ professional security analysis skills. These are recommended manually for security-critical projects rather than auto-installed, as they significantly expand the agent's security analysis scope.

## Permissions & Safety

Permissions & Safety
VibeCrew uses a defense-in-depth model with three layers of protection. Before any agent action reaches your filesystem, it passes through permission rules, hook guards, and quality gates. This means the AI can work productively without asking for permission every 5 seconds, while being physically unable to do anything destructive.
&#9632;
What it is
Three concentric safety layers: settings.json (allow and deny rules), PreToolUse hook scripts (phase gate, path restrictions, destructive command blocking), and Stop hook quality gates (typecheck, lint, build, cost limits).
&#10003;
What problem it solves
AI agents can attempt risky actions — force-pushing, deleting files, running as root, or writing code before architecture is decided. VibeCrew blocks these deterministically with bash scripts, not by hoping the model remembers the rules.
Allowed without prompts
File operations — Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep
npm scripts — test, lint, build, format, type-check
Git — status, log, diff, add, commit, checkout, branch, worktree, revert, tags
GitHub/GitLab CLI — PR create/list/view, pipeline view
Shell utilities — jq, cat, ls, wc, sort, head, tail, mkdir, cp, mv
Security audits — npm audit, pip audit, cargo audit, govulncheck
Always blocked
Privilege escalation — sudo, su, doas, pkexec
Force operations — git push --force, git reset --hard, git clean -f
Destructive commands — rm -rf /, rm -rf ~, chmod 777
System modifications — npm install -g, kill -9, systemctl, crontab
Data destruction — DROP TABLE, DELETE FROM without WHERE (hook layer)
Path violations — writes outside project root, source code before foundation

## Personalization

On This Page
How the Profile System Works

The Profile Interview
How Agents Adapt

Changing Your Profile
How the Profile System Works
Most AI coding tools treat every user the same. A junior developer gets the same unexplained terminal output as a senior engineer. A learner is overwhelmed by terse error messages. An experienced developer wades through verbose explanations they don't need. VibeCrew's profile system solves this by adapting every agent's behavior to your experience level, working style, and preferences.
&#9632;
What it is
A multi-dimension preference system that controls how every agent communicates, how much autonomy the system takes, how technical the language is, and how adventurous technology choices are.
&#10003;
What problem it solves
A founder who can't read code needs walkthrough PRs with plain English. A senior developer wants minimal output and full autonomy. The profile ensures both get exactly the experience they need — without either having to fight the defaults.
&#9888;
Completely optional
If you skip the profile interview, every agent uses sensible defaults (checkpoints autonomy, standard verbosity, balanced risk). You can run /profile at any time — or change settings directly in the dashboard.
Dimensions
Each dimension controls a different axis of the system's behavior. Together they create a unique experience tailored to your needs.
&#128214;
Code Literacy
How technical the language in reviews, errors, docs, and commit messages is.
Fluent — technical jargon used freely, minimal comments
Conversational — brief definitions for domain jargon
Basic — plain English comments on exports and complex logic
None — every export gets JSDoc, error messages include plain-language explanations
&#127918;
Autonomy
How much VibeCrew does on its own before asking for approval.
Full Auto — make decisions and keep going, only stop when blocked
Checkpoints — check in at major decisions (tech stack, design, merge)
Collaborative — explain each step, user understands and approves
Supervised — ask before every significant action, full control
&#128203;
PR Review
How code changes are packaged and merged.
Auto-merge — merge after tests pass, skip PRs entirely
Summary — PR with a brief 3-line summary
Review — detailed PR with quality gate table and test plan
Walkthrough — line-by-line explanations of every change
&#128172;
Verbosity
How much detail you get in messages, coaching, and session summaries.
Minimal — just the facts: status, errors, done
Standard — brief explanations of what happened and what's next
Detailed — decisions, trade-offs, and alternatives explained
Educational — teaches concepts and patterns as you go
&#127942;
Gamification
How much of the progression system (XP, badges, streaks) is visible.
All In — show everything: XP, levels, badges, streaks, challenges
Light Touch — show level and score, skip badges/streaks
Score Only — just the Vibe Score, nothing else
Disabled — no gamification output at all
&#127891;
Learning Style
How the system helps you understand your project's codebase.
Don't Explain — just build, user reads the code themselves
Reference Docs — generate documentation to read later
Inline — comments in code, explanations in commits
Teach Me — explain concepts interactively, full understanding
&#9878;
Risk Tolerance
How adventurous technology choices are during TDR research.
Conservative — proven, battle-tested technologies (3+ years, major backing)
Balanced — modern but established, no bleeding-edge or legacy
Progressive — newer technologies if they offer clear advantages
Experimental — latest and greatest, accepts the risk
The Profile Interview
Running /profile starts an interactive interview — 7 quick questions that take about 2 minutes. The interview is conversational: you can answer with a number (1&ndash;4) or describe what you want in plain text.
Interview Flow
StepQuestionSmart Behavior
1How comfortable are you reading code?Calibrates how technical the system's language will be.
2How much should VibeCrew do on its own?Controls approval gates across the entire workflow.
3How should code changes be merged?Determines PR detail level — from auto-merge to line-by-line walkthroughs.
4How much detail do you want in messages?Affects every agent's output length and explanation depth.
5Do you enjoy gamification?Automatically syncs the gamification config (XP display, streak reminders, badges).
6How do you want to learn about your codebase?Controls documentation depth and whether code gets explanatory comments.
7What's your approach to technology choices?Steers the Stack Scout toward stable or cutting-edge technologies.
If you already have a profile, /profile shows your current settings first and asks which dimensions you want to change. You don't have to redo the whole interview.
How Agents Adapt
Every profile-aware agent calls read-profile.sh on startup to load your preferences. Here's exactly what changes for each agent based on your profile.
Session Startup
Reads verbosity to control greeting depth.
VerbosityGreeting
Minimal4-line banner only. No hints, no handoff summary.
StandardBanner + onboarding hint (e.g., "Tip: Run /profile to personalize VibeCrew")
DetailedBanner + hint + one-line project context summary
EducationalBanner + hint + context + "Did you know?" tip about unused features
Workflow Orchestrator
Reads autonomy and verbosity to control approval gates and explanation depth.
ComponentFull AutoCheckpointsCollaborativeSupervised
Foundation artifactsAuto-approve allApprove per artifactExplain then approveShow examples, explain reasoning
TDR decisionsAuto-select bestRecommend + approveSide-by-side comparisonFull debate matrix
Phase transitionsSilentAnnounceExplain next phaseInteractive walkthrough
/run-backlog pausesNo pausesPause per featurePause per phasePause per action
Error recoveryAuto-fix 3xAuto-fix 1x, then askShow error, ask approachExplain all options
Builder
Reads verbosity, code_literacy, and pr_review to shape code output.
AspectDimensionAdaptation
Commit messagesverbosityMinimal: type(scope) only. Standard: + bullet list. Detailed: + rationale. Educational: + design pattern explanation.
Code commentscode_literacyFluent: minimal, non-obvious logic only. None: every export gets JSDoc, complex blocks get inline annotations.
PR bodypr_reviewAuto-merge: auto-merge label. Summary: 3 lines. Review: full quality gate table. Walkthrough: + per-file code walkthrough.
Verifier
Reads verbosity and gamification_preference for coaching output.
AspectDimensionAdaptation
/wrap outputverbosityMinimal: score + rating only. Standard: + coaching suggestions. Detailed: full deduction/bonus breakdown. Educational: + "Learning moment".
Progression displaygamificationFull: XP, levels, badges, streaks, challenges. Light: level + XP only. Score only: Vibe Score. Disabled: no gamification framing.
Stack Scout
Reads risk_tolerance to weight technology maturity in TDR research.
Risk ToleranceTechnology Selection Criteria
Conservative3+ years production use, 100k+ npm weekly downloads, major company backing. Exclude technologies under 2 years old.
BalancedModern but established. Standard comparison across maturity, DX, and community.
ProgressiveConsider 1&ndash;2 year old technologies if they offer clear advantages. Include benchmarks.
ExperimentalSeek cutting-edge options. Include alpha/beta-stage technologies. Add "Migration if this fails" section to TDR.
Code Reviewer
Reads code_literacy and pr_review to adjust finding explanations and review thoroughness.
AspectDimensionAdaptation
Finding languagecode_literacyFluent: technical terminology, brief findings. Conversational: adds context parentheticals. Basic: plain English with before/after. None: non-technical language, grouped by impact.
Review depthpr_reviewAuto-merge: critical only (security, correctness). Summary: + light convention check. Review: full 10-step review. Walkthrough: + per-file code walkthrough.
Doc Generator
Reads learning and code_literacy to shape documentation style.
AspectDimensionAdaptation
Doc depthlearningDon't Explain: minimal maintainability docs. Reference: comprehensive with API references. Inline: + JSDoc flagging. Teach: + "How it works" sections with Mermaid diagrams.
Doc languagecode_literacyFluent: idiomatic code examples. Conversational: parenthetical definitions. Basic: analogies instead of jargon. None: non-technical guide, annotated code.
Storage & Scripts
Your profile is stored as JSON in .vibecrew/config.json under the user_profile key. Two bash scripts handle all reads and writes.
Profile Scripts
ScriptPurposeKey Behavior
read-profile.sh
Universal profile reader called by all agents
Merges stored profile over defaults so missing fields are always filled. Always exits 0 — returns defaults if no profile exists. Single bash call, ~500 tokens.
save-profile.sh
Writes profile and syncs gamification config
Atomic writes via PID-suffixed temp files. Validates config.json exists. Sets interview_completed: true and updated_at timestamp. Uses advisory locks for concurrent safety.
Gamification Sync
When you change the gamification preference, save-profile.sh automatically syncs three related config flags:
Preferenceenabledshow_xp_in_statusstreak_reminders
Fulltruetruetrue
Lighttruetruefalse
Score Onlytruefalsefalse
Disabledfalsefalsefalse
Changing Your Profile
Your profile isn't locked in. As your experience grows and your needs change, you have two ways to update it.
CLI: /profile
Run /profile in any session. If you already have a profile, it shows your current settings and asks which dimensions you want to change. The conversational interview makes it easy to adjust one or all dimensions without starting from scratch.
Dashboard: Settings Tab
Open your project's Vibe Dashboard and navigate to the Settings tab. The browser-based editor lets you modify any profile dimension with dropdowns, see the effect immediately, and save. Changes write directly to .vibecrew/config.json.
Both methods write to the same config.json file. Changes take effect immediately — the next agent that runs will read your updated preferences.
A learner who started with educational verbosity and collaborative autonomy might switch to standard and checkpoints after a few projects. A founder who initially needed walkthrough PRs might move to summary PRs once they're comfortable with the process. Revisit your profile whenever your workflow feels too noisy or too quiet.
Example: A Founder's Journey
StageProfile ChangesWhy
Week 1
Autonomy: supervised, Verbosity: educational, PR: walkthrough
Learning how everything works. Wants full explanations and control.
Month 1
Autonomy: collaborative, Verbosity: detailed, PR: review
Understands the workflow. Still wants to approve decisions but doesn't need hand-holding.
Month 3
Autonomy: checkpoints, Verbosity: standard, PR: summary
Trusts the system. Only pauses at major decisions. Reads summaries instead of walkthroughs.
Agent Overlay Customization
Beyond profiles, you can customize individual agent behavior per-project by creating override files
in .vibecrew/agent-overrides/<agent>.md. Overrides survive plugin updates because
they live in your project directory, not the plugin.
AspectHow It Works
Section replacementOverride sections with matching ## Heading names replace the base section entirely
Section appendNew headings in the override are appended after all base sections
Frontmatter preservedModel, tools, isolation, and maxTurns cannot be changed by overrides
Empty/missingNo override file = base agent used unchanged
Example: To make the Builder always use Prisma ORM and CSS Modules for a specific project,
create .vibecrew/agent-overrides/builder.md with custom ## Code Phase and
## Project-Specific Conventions sections.

## Plugin Structure

Plugin Structure
VibeCrew is a Claude Code plugin — an add-on that gives Claude Code new abilities. When you open a project with VibeCrew installed, Claude Code reads a manifest file and automatically loads agents, skills, hooks, scripts, MCP servers, and permissions. Everything lives inside the claude-plugin-vibe-crew/ directory.
&#9632;
What it is
A self-contained folder with a plugin.json manifest that registers agents, slash commands, hooks, scripts, and MCP servers — everything the system needs in one install.
&#10003;
What problem it solves
Without a plugin, you'd manually configure each agent, permission rule, and automation script for every project. The plugin bundles everything into a single install.
Plugin Components
ComponentFile / DirectoryWhat It Does
Plugin Manifest
.claude-plugin/plugin.json
Entry point that Claude Code reads on startup. Registers every agent, skill, hook binding, and MCP server so they load automatically.
MCP Servers
.mcp.json
Configures external tool servers (Context7, Chrome DevTools, Playwright, and conditionally Semgrep, Sentry, Supabase, Stripe, Vercel, Figma) that give agents web search, browser control, and service integrations.
Permissions
settings.json
Allow/deny rules that control what agents can do without prompting. Allows file ops, npm scripts, and git; blocks sudo, force push, and destructive commands.
Hooks
hooks/hooks.json
Event bindings that map Claude Code lifecycle events (session start, tool use, stop) to bash scripts that enforce rules at zero token cost.
Scripts
scripts/
Bash programs that handle mechanical work: state mutations, scoring, git operations, notifications, formatting, and project analysis.
Agents
agents/
System prompt files that define each specialized AI agent's role, tools, constraints, and output format.
Skills
skills/
Slash command definitions as SKILL.md files. Each contains YAML metadata and a workflow body that routes to the right agent(s).
Templates
templates/
Project scaffolding templates, doc-site scaffold, and an MCP registry of additional servers that can be auto-discovered from TDR technology choices.
Tests
tests/
BATS test suite that validates hook scripts, state management, and core plugin behavior.

---

## Runtime State

Runtime State
Every project using VibeCrew gets a .vibecrew/ folder that stores all runtime state: project configuration, foundation progress, feature backlog, session logs, Vibe Scores, architecture diagrams, and cross-session handoffs. This folder is the system's memory — it persists between sessions and lets agents pick up exactly where the last one left off.
&#9632;
What it is
A directory of JSON files and sub-folders created by /setup. Core files: config.json (preferences), state.json (current phase), backlog.json (feature specs), gamification.json (progression). Sub-directories hold sessions, scores, signals, locks, and architecture diagrams.
&#10003;
What problem it solves
AI sessions are stateless — each new conversation starts from scratch. The .vibecrew/ folder gives the system persistent memory: which features are done, what phase you're in, your quality trends, and even architectural diagrams that agents reference instead of re-deriving structure from code.
Core State Files
JSON files that store project configuration and progress.
FileRead ByWhat It Stores
config.json
All agents, hooks, status bar
Terminal preferences, notification settings, user profile (role, verbosity, autonomy, etc.), cost thresholds, and MCP server toggles.
state.json
All agents, hooks, status bar
Foundation completion status, active feature name, current phase, plan revision count, feature history, and last session timestamp.
backlog.json
Orchestrator, Builder, dashboard
Feature specifications with Kanban columns (Ideas → Planned → In Progress → Testing → Review → Done), priority, complexity (trivial/standard/complex), milestones, and acceptance criteria.
gamification.json
Performance Coach, dashboard
XP, level, earned badges, skill tree progress, active streaks, and challenge completions. Opt-in via /profile.
Runtime Directories
Sub-directories that store session data and inter-agent communication.
DirectoryWhat It StoresWho Uses It
architecture/
5 Mermaid .mmd files: system topology, ER schema, state flows, API sequences, and component tree.
Builder (reads for context), Doc Generator (freshness check), injected once per session.
sessions/
JSON logs for each session: start/end time, features worked on, Vibe Score, token usage, cost.
Performance Coach (trend analysis), dashboard (stats/trends tabs).
scores/
Detailed Vibe Score breakdowns: each deduction and bonus with reasons.
Performance Coach, dashboard (trends tab), status bar (current score).
signals/
Inter-agent signal files for communication between worktree agents and the main session.
Agents (write signals), hooks (validate schema before write).
locks/
Advisory lock files that prevent concurrent modifications to shared state.
Scripts (acquire/release), error recovery (clear stale locks).
handoffs/
Structured context transfer documents created by /handoff for cross-session continuity.
Session Startup (detects and loads), agents (reads for context).
analysis/
4 persistent markdown files from /onboard: stack.md (language, framework, deps), architecture.md (dirs, patterns, API style), conventions.md (formatting, naming, test patterns), gaps.md (coverage, untested modules, TODOs). Refreshable via /onboard --refresh.
Builder (Plan phase injection), compact-reinject (post-compaction context), Session Startup (staleness check).
releases/
Release notes data (JSON) with version history and feature summaries.
Doc Generator (/release), dashboard releases tab.
workflows/
Reusable workflow templates extracted from high-scoring sessions via /replay.
Orchestrator (loads templates for replay).
expertise/
Persistent agent expertise records — learned patterns and session learnings (JSON).
Performance Coach (writes), Builder and Code Reviewer (read for adaptive behavior).
memory/
Per-agent persistent memory — operational knowledge accumulated across sessions (JSONL). Organized as memory/<agent>/<domain>.jsonl with TTL-based auto-pruning.
Builder (API patterns, conventions), Verifier (flaky tests), Stack Scout (library gotchas), Code Reviewer (recurring issues).
agent-overrides/
Per-project agent customization files (<agent>.md). Sections with matching headings replace the base agent&rsquo;s sections; new headings are appended. Frontmatter (model, tools, isolation) is always preserved from the base agent. Survives plugin updates.
All agents (loaded via load-agent-with-overrides.sh at agent start).

---

## Self-Improving System

Self-Improving System
VibeCrew doesn't just build software — it learns from every session. The Performance Coach analyzes each session's patterns, proposes permanent rule changes to CLAUDE.md, and aggregates anonymized metrics across all your projects. Each session makes the next one better.
&#9632;
What it is
A feedback loop: the Performance Coach scores each session, detects anti-patterns, and proposes CLAUDE.md mutations. Cross-project telemetry tracks trends across all your VibeCrew projects. The /system-review command analyzes the plugin's own performance.
&#10003;
What problem it solves
AI agents make the same mistakes across sessions because they start fresh each time. The self-improving loop captures what went wrong (and right), encodes fixes as permanent CLAUDE.md rules, and tracks whether those fixes actually work over time.
Performance Coach
The Performance Coach is an Opus agent that runs during /wrap at the end of every session. It analyzes what happened during the session and produces actionable coaching.
What It Analyzes
DimensionWhat It ChecksExample Finding
Prompt Efficiency
Prompt churn (repeated similar prompts), tool loops (same tool called 3+ times)
"You re-prompted the Builder 4 times for the same component — next time, include acceptance criteria in the spec."
Cache Utilization
Cache hit ratio across the session
"Cache utilization was 23% — consider keeping CLAUDE.md stable to improve prompt caching."
Phase Completeness
Missing artifacts (tests, docs, review) for each phase
"Feature shipped without E2E tests — consider adding /e2e to your workflow."
Context Discipline
Context window usage at session end, number of compactions
"Session hit 82% context usage — offload research to Stack Scout earlier."
Anti-patterns
Recurring mistakes across 3+ sessions
"This is the 3rd session with skipped code review — proposing a CLAUDE.md rule to make review mandatory."
Vibe Score
Every session receives a quality score from 0 to 130. The score starts at 100 and applies deductions for problems and bonuses for excellence. The Performance Coach uses score trends to identify coaching opportunities.
Deductions
IssuePenaltyWhat Triggers It
Prompt churn-5 per sequence3+ similar prompts to the same agent without meaningful change
Tool loops-10 per loopSame tool called repeatedly without progress
Low cache utilization-15Cache hit ratio below 30%
Context violations-20Session exceeded 60% context usage
No tests-10Feature completed without any test files
No feature spec-5Feature started without a spec in backlog.json
Skipped code review-5Feature wrapped without running /review
Documentation drift-3 per stale docSource code changed but matching docs not updated
Console errors-5Browser console errors on affected pages
Visual token violations-3 per violation (max -9)Design system tokens used incorrectly
Unresolved clarifications&minus;3Plan phase identified 3+ ambiguities that went unresolved (low-confidence assumptions in code).
Bonuses
AchievementBonusWhat Triggers It
Complete phase artifacts+5All 6 phases have their required artifacts
High cache utilization+5Cache hit ratio above 60%
Full test coverage+5All modified files have corresponding tests
Clean session+5No tool loops, no prompt churn, no context violations
TDD discipline+3Tests written before implementation code
E2E tests passing+3Playwright E2E tests run and pass
Accessibility clean+2No axe-core violations found
Code review complete+2/review ran with all findings addressed
Performance baselines+2k6 performance tests run with baselines set
Visual compliance clean+3No design system token violations
Plan Staleness Detection
During the Code phase, check-plan-staleness.sh compares files referenced in plan.md against the plan's commit SHA. If source files have changed since the plan was written, the script assesses severity and recommends action.
Severity Levels
SeverityCriteriaRecommendation
noneNo plan-referenced files changed since plan commitProceed normally
minor1&ndash;2 files changed, <50 lines totalReview changes, then proceed
major3+ files changed or >50 lines modifiedRefresh the plan before continuing
criticalPlan-referenced file deleted or renamedRefresh the plan (mandatory)
Vibe Score Integration
The plan_revision_count field in state.json tracks how often specs change mid-feature. Frequent plan revisions indicate unstable requirements and reduce the session's Vibe Score. The Performance Coach monitors this metric across sessions to detect planning pattern issues.
Erosion & Drift Tracking
VibeCrew monitors two forms of session degradation: drift (agents exploring instead of progressing) and code erosion (increasing complexity metrics over time).
Drift Tracking
A two-tier system detects when agents spend too much time exploring rather than making progress.
PhaseSoft Warning(drift-tracker.sh)Hard Escalation(drift-circuit-breaker.sh)
Plan40 exploration calls60 exploration calls
Design30 exploration calls45 exploration calls
Code20 exploration calls35 exploration calls
Test15 exploration calls25 exploration calls
Docs15 exploration calls25 exploration calls
Soft warnings are emitted by drift-tracker.sh (PostToolUse hook) and never block. Hard escalation via drift-circuit-breaker.sh (Stop hook) creates a WIP commit and blocker signal, prompting the agent to change approach. The circuit breaker is fail-open — it never prevents a session from stopping.
Code Erosion
collect-erosion-metrics.sh gathers complexity metrics (lines of code, cyclomatic complexity, function length, import count) and calculate-erosion-score.sh computes a 0&ndash;100 erosion score.
Score RangeRatingVibe Score Impact
80&ndash;100Healthy+2 bonus
60&ndash;79ModerateNo impact
40&ndash;59Concerning&minus;3 deduction
0&ndash;39Critical&minus;5 deduction
Session Learnings & CLAUDE.md Mutations
When the Performance Coach detects a recurring anti-pattern (appears in 3+ sessions), it proposes a permanent rule change to the project's CLAUDE.md file. These mutations are the mechanism by which VibeCrew gets smarter over time.
How Mutations Work
StepWhat Happens
1. DetectionPerformance Coach identifies a pattern appearing in 3+ sessions (e.g., "tests always written after code" or "docs consistently skipped").
2. ProposalCoach drafts a concrete CLAUDE.md rule using a standard template. Example: "Always run /tdd before implementing — write the test first."
3. ApprovalThe proposal is shown to the user for approval. Mutations never auto-apply — the user always has final say.
4. Applicationapply-mutation.sh appends the rule to the Session Learnings section of CLAUDE.md.
5. PruningSession Learnings are capped at 15 entries. When a new rule is added past the limit, the oldest entry is removed to keep CLAUDE.md lean.
&#9888;
Why 15 learnings max?
Research shows oversized CLAUDE.md files increase agent cost 20%+ without improving success rates. The cap ensures the file stays under 200 lines. Old learnings that haven't prevented their anti-pattern get pruned first.
Cross-Project Telemetry
VibeCrew tracks anonymized performance data across all your projects. This isn't sent anywhere — it lives locally in the plugin directory and powers the /system-review command.
How It Works
StepWhat Happens
Auto-registrationDuring /setup, the project registers itself in the central plugin's project-registry.json. Project paths are replaced with anonymous aliases (project-001, project-002).
Data collectionAfter each /wrap, anonymized metrics (Vibe Score, agent usage, token counts, cost) are appended to telemetry/aggregate.json in the plugin directory.
Aggregation/system-review reads all registered projects' telemetry to compute cross-project trends: average scores, most-used agents, cost patterns, MCP adoption rates.
What /system-review Shows
SectionWhat It Contains
Score TrendsAverage Vibe Score trajectory across all projects — are you getting better over time?
Agent UsageWhich agents are used most, which are underutilized, and cost breakdown by agent.
Cost AnalysisPer-project and aggregate cost metrics. Identifies expensive patterns and cost-saving opportunities.
MCP AdoptionWhich MCP servers are active across projects and their impact on session efficiency.
Ecosystem ResearchThe System Reviewer agent checks for VibeCrew updates, new MCP servers, and community best practices.
Agent Persistent Memory
Some agents maintain persistent memory across sessions using two complementary mechanisms. This allows agents to learn from previous runs without relying solely on CLAUDE.md mutations.
Three Learning Mechanisms
MechanismStorageScopeUsed By
Performance Coach Mutations
CLAUDE.md rules
All agents (global)
Performance Coach
Expertise Records
.vibecrew/expertise/ JSON
Cross-agent (structured)
Builder, Code Reviewer
Agent Memory
.vibecrew/memory/
Agent-private (free-form)
Performance Coach, Code Simplifier, Security Auditor
&#9632;
Why three mechanisms?
Each serves a different purpose: CLAUDE.md mutations encode global rules that all agents follow. Expertise records store structured, queryable data (conventions, failure patterns, decisions) shared across agents. Agent memory stores private, free-form notes for unstructured learnings specific to one agent.
Skill Evaluation & Model-Change Resilience
VibeCrew tracks whether its skills remain effective as models improve. The /validate-skills command evaluates skill health, and model-change detection at session startup alerts you when re-evaluation is needed.
The Evaluation Loop
StepWhat Happens
1. DetectionSession startup compares the current model against .last-validated-model.txt. If changed, a one-line warning fires.
2. Evaluation/validate-skills runs 3-tier analysis: schema check, model-version tracking, and A/B test recommendations.
3. TestingCapability-uplift skills (analysis + action categories) are flagged for A/B testing via Skill Creator.
4. TrackingResults stored in .vibecrew/reviews/skill-health-*.json with model version and validation date.
Skill Categories
CategoryMaintenance Strategy
workflowDurable — encodes preferences, optimize triggers
analysisCapability-uplift — A/B test after model upgrades
actionCapability-uplift — A/B test after model upgrades
dashboardDurable — read-only, optimize for speed
utilityDurable — simple operations, minimal maintenance
&#10003;
Schema Validation Hook
The validate-skill-schema.sh PostToolUse hook automatically validates every SKILL.md write. It checks required fields, category values, and context: fork / agent: pairing — catching schema errors before they reach production.
Regression Test Feedback Loop
When a bug fix (fix: commit) is made without an accompanying test, VibeCrew automatically generates a regression test skeleton to prevent the bug from recurring. This closes the gap between bug fixes and test coverage.
How It Works
StepWhat Happens
1. DetectionDuring /wrap, detect-fix-commits.sh scans the session's git log for fix: conventional commits. For each, it checks whether the same commit also modified test files.
2. GenerationIf no test changes accompany the fix, generate-regression-test.sh creates a test skeleton in the appropriate framework (BATS for bash scripts, Vitest/Jest for TypeScript projects). Skeletons include a skip marker for developers to fill in.
3. ScoringThe Vibe Score applies a -5 deduction per fix commit without a regression test (fix-without-regression). Fix commits with tests get no deduction.
4. ExpertiseBug-fix patterns are stored in the expertise knowledge base (domain: failures) for cross-session analysis of recurring bug categories.
5. MutationAfter 3+ sessions with uncovered fix commits, the Performance Coach proposes a CLAUDE.md rule: "When fixing a bug, always add a regression test that reproduces the original failure."
<MermaidDiagram chart={`flowchart LR
A["fix: commit"] --> B{"Test fileschanged?"}
B -->|No| C["detect-fix-commits.sh"]
C --> D["generate-regression-test.sh"]
D --> AP{"Userapproves?"}
AP -->|Yes| E["Skeleton committed"]
AP -->|No| F["-5 Vibe Score"]
C --> F["-5 Vibe Score"]
B -->|Yes| G["No action"]
G --> H["Neutral score"]
E --> EX["expertise-write.sh(domain: failures)"]
F --> I["3+ sessions?"]
I -->|Yes| J["CLAUDE.md mutationproposed"]
I -->|No| K["Logged forfuture tracking"]
style A fill:#fde8e8,stroke:#333
style AP fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#333
style E fill:#e8fde8,stroke:#333
style G fill:#e8fde8,stroke:#333

style J fill:#e8e8fd,stroke:#333
style EX fill:#e8e8fd,stroke:#333`}
caption="Bug fixes without tests trigger scoring deductions (computed independently by calculate-vibe-score.sh), skeleton generation with user approval, expertise recording, and eventually a permanent CLAUDE.md rule."
/>
The Self-Improvement Loop
Every session feeds back into the system, making the next session more efficient. The loop runs automatically during /wrap — no manual intervention required.

## Skills Reference

Skills Reference
Every slash command maps to a skill — a SKILL.md file in the skills/ directory. Skills range from zero-cost script-only operations (like /idea and /status) to complex multi-agent orchestrations (like /new-project and /wrap). Use the category filters to browse all available skills.
&#9632;
What they are
SKILL.md files with YAML frontmatter (name, description, arguments) and a markdown body defining the full workflow: preconditions, steps, error handling, and agent routing. Some skills are script-only (zero tokens), others spin up single or multiple agents.
&#10003;
What problem they solve
Skills turn complex multi-step workflows into single commands. Instead of writing a detailed prompt for "run tests, calculate score, generate docs, commit, and log session," you type /wrap and the skill definition handles every step, error path, and agent handoff.
Modern Skill Patterns
VibeCrew skills leverage advanced Claude Code features for better autocomplete, cost optimization, tool scoping, and native subagent isolation.
Frontmatter Fields
FieldPurposeExample
argument-hintShows placeholder text in autocomplete after the skill name"User Authentication"
allowed-toolsRestricts which tools the skill can use — enforces read-only for dashboardsRead, Bash, Glob, Grep
modelRoutes skill to a specific model for cost optimizationhaiku for dashboards
context: forkRuns the skill as an isolated subagent — results return to main sessionUsed by /review, /audit
agent:Specifies which agent runs in a forked contextcode-reviewer
categoryClassifies skill for evaluation and retirement trackingworkflow, analysis, action
Dynamic Injection (! Backtick)
Skills can pre-load data at load time using ! backtick syntax. The shell command runs before Claude sees the prompt, eliminating the first &ldquo;read state&rdquo; turn and saving tokens.
SkillWhat Gets Injected
/statusstate.json, backlog.json, git branch, recent commits, latest score
/costSession cost data, aggregated spending
/checkpackage.json (scripts section)
/wrapstate.json, backlog.json, git diff --stat
/fix-issueGit provider auth check
/healCI logs, provider auth check
Native Argument Substitution
Skills use $ARGUMENTS and $0 for native argument parsing instead of manual extraction steps. $0 captures the first argument, $ARGUMENTS captures the full argument string.
Forked Skills
Four analysis skills use context: fork with a dedicated agent: to run in native subagent isolation. The forked agent produces formatted output directly and returns results to the main session.
SkillAgentWhy Forked
/reviewCode ReviewerRead-only analysis — clean single-agent scope
/simplifyCode SimplifierAnalysis-only; /apply-simplifications handles interactive changes
/auditSecurity AuditorOWASP scan with pre-injected dependency + secret data
/system-reviewSystem ReviewerCross-project telemetry analysis
Intent-Based Triggering
You don&apos;t need to memorize all 38 commands. VibeCrew includes an intent detection layer that matches
natural language to the right skill. For example, saying &ldquo;fix a bug&rdquo; suggests /fix-issue,
and &ldquo;check quality&rdquo; suggests /check. Intent detection runs automatically during
session startup and when the Orchestrator processes your requests.
The full mapping is defined in templates/intent-map.md and covers all core workflows:
project setup, planning, development, quality, session management, CI/CD, analysis, and gamification.
Slash commands remain the primary interface — intent detection is a convenience layer for discoverability.
Skill Categories
Every skill has a category field that determines its evaluation strategy and retirement criteria.
CategoryCountEvaluation Strategy
workflow7 skillsDurable (preference-encoding) — optimize triggers, rarely retire
analysis6 skillsCapability-uplift — A/B test after model upgrades
action8 skillsCapability-uplift — A/B test after model upgrades
dashboard4 skillsDurable — read-only, optimize for speed
utility10 skillsDurable — simple operations, minimal maintenance

## Slash Commands

Slash Commands
Slash commands are the primary user interface to VibeCrew. You type a command starting with / and the system handles the rest. Each command is defined as a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter (name, description, arguments) and a markdown body containing the full workflow: preconditions, steps, error handling, and agent handoffs.
&#9632;
What they are
Commands across several categories: setup, planning, development, quality, safety, session management, and gamification. Some are script-only (zero token cost), others orchestrate multiple agents.
&#10003;
What problem they solve
Without slash commands, you'd need to manually prompt the AI with detailed instructions for every workflow step. Commands encode expert workflows into one-word triggers — /wrap runs quality checks, scores your session, generates docs, and commits, all automatically.
Setup & Onboarding
Run these once when starting a new project or joining an existing one.
CommandWhat It DoesWhen to Use
/setup
Verifies dependencies (Git, Node, jq), detects your terminal, and creates the .vibecrew/ folder.
First thing you run in any project. Tells you if anything is missing.
/new-project
Runs the full 7-step foundation: VISION.md, design system, TDR, architecture diagrams, roadmap, and CLAUDE.md.
Starting a brand-new project from scratch. This is the Tier 1 workflow.
/onboard
Analyzes an existing codebase — extracts conventions, tech stack, generates a CLAUDE.md, and creates persistent analysis docs (.vibecrew/analysis/). Use --refresh to re-run analysis and regenerate analysis docs without repeating full onboarding.
Adding VibeCrew to a project that already has code. Use --refresh when the codebase has changed significantly.
/profile
Interview (or preset selection) that configures how agents communicate and work with you.
After setup, to personalize agent behavior for your experience level and preferences.
/install-skill <source>
Install companion skills from GitHub repos, local paths, or company-internal sources. Runs 5-gate safety validation on remote sources.
After TDR approval when companion skills are recommended, or anytime you want to add a skill manually.
Planning
Define what to build and track progress.
CommandWhat It DoesWhen to Use
/plan-features
Interactive session to define backlog specs: problem statement, acceptance criteria, priority, complexity, dependencies.
After foundation is complete, to define what features you want to build.
/idea "text"
Captures a one-line idea to backlog.json with status "unplanned". Zero AI cost.
Anytime you have a feature idea — quick capture without breaking your flow.
/status
Full project dashboard: foundation progress, backlog overview, active feature, recent Vibe Scores, and a &ldquo;What Next?&rdquo; recommendation based on current state.
To see where your project stands at a glance. Script-only, no token cost.
/sync-issues
Imports open GitHub/GitLab issues by label into the VibeCrew backlog.
To pull external issue tracker items into VibeCrew for execution.
Development
Build features and fix bugs.
CommandWhat It DoesWhen to Use
/new-feature "name"
Creates a branch, checkpoint, and starts the 6-phase development cycle (Plan → UI Design → Code → Test → Review → Docs).
To start building a planned feature. One feature at a time (WIP limit enforced).
/run-backlog
Automatically executes features from the backlog by priority. Stops on failure for human review.
When you want VibeCrew to work through multiple features autonomously.
/check
Runs tests, build, lint, and type-check without modifying any code.
Quick health check at any time during development.
/debug
Structured debugging with hypothesis testing, variable inspection, and root cause analysis.
When something is broken and you need a methodical investigation.
/fix-issue <number>
Fetches a GitHub/GitLab issue, diagnoses the problem, implements a fix, tests it, and creates a PR/MR.
To fix a specific issue end-to-end from your issue tracker.
/quick "description"
Fast-track small fixes: pre-flight check, scope guard (warns if it looks like a feature), implement, quality gate, conventional commit, session log. No backlog entry, no feature branch, no Vibe Score.
For typo fixes, config tweaks, and other changes too small for the full feature cycle.
Testing & Review
Validate quality, security, and accessibility.
CommandWhat It DoesWhen to Use
/review
Code review against feature spec, TDR compliance, and conventions. Findings grouped by severity.
After coding is done, before wrapping up a feature.
/tdd
Test-driven development cycle: write a failing test first, then implement until it passes.
When you want to develop using the red-green-refactor pattern.
/e2e
Generates Playwright end-to-end tests with Page Object Model patterns.
To add browser-level integration tests for user flows.
/perf-test
Generates k6 load, stress, spike, and soak test suites.
To benchmark API performance and find bottlenecks under load.
/a11y
WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility audit via axe-core.
To check your UI for accessibility issues before shipping.
Quality & Analysis
Improve code quality and challenge decisions.
CommandWhat It DoesWhen to Use
/simplify
Read-only analysis: finds dead code, over-abstractions, and API surface bloat. You approve each change.
When code feels complex or after a big feature to reduce technical debt.
/apply-simplifications
Applies the changes you approved from the /simplify analysis.
After reviewing /simplify results and selecting what to apply.
/reconsider
Devil's advocate analysis of TDR decisions with debate matrices and risk assessments.
When you want a second opinion on architectural or technology choices.
/replay
Create, list, or apply workflow templates from high-scoring sessions.
To reuse a proven workflow pattern from a previous successful session.
/system-review
Plugin meta-analysis, cross-project telemetry, and ecosystem research.
To analyze VibeCrew's own performance across all your projects.
/validate-skills
Evaluate skill schema quality, model-version tracking, and A/B test recommendations across 3 tiers.
After model updates or when skill reliability degrades. Periodic health check.
Safety
Monitor costs, audit security, and fix CI.
CommandWhat It DoesWhen to Use
/audit
OWASP Top 10 security scan: injection, auth, XSS, secrets, dependency vulnerabilities.
Before shipping to production, or periodically to catch security issues.
/heal
Fetches CI logs, diagnoses the failure, and applies a fix (max 3 attempts).
When your CI pipeline is failing and you need automated diagnosis.
/cost
Real-time cost dashboard: session, daily, weekly, and monthly aggregates with pricing table.
To check how much you've spent on AI tokens. Script-only, no token cost.
/undo
Lists checkpoints and recent commits, lets you safely revert or reset.
When something went wrong and you need to roll back changes.
Session Management
Wrap up work and transfer context between sessions.
CommandWhat It DoesWhen to Use
/wrap
Quality gate, Vibe Score calculation, performance coaching, commit, session log, and gamification pipeline.
At the end of every session. This is how VibeCrew scores and records your work.
/handoff
Generates a structured context transfer document for the next session.
When you're stopping mid-feature and need the next session to pick up exactly where you left off.
/release
Generates release notes from git history and session logs.
When you're ready to publish a new version of your project.
/recover-state
Clears lock files and repairs corrupted JSON state.
When VibeCrew is stuck or state files are broken after a crash.
Gamification
Track progress, earn rewards, and test your knowledge.
CommandWhat It DoesWhen to Use
/achievements
Shows your level, badges, skill tree, streaks, and active challenges.
Anytime you want to see your progress. Links to the visual dashboard.
/quiz
Interactive knowledge checks with educational explanations. Unlocks at Level 3.
To test and improve your understanding of your project's codebase and tools.

## Status Line

On This Page
What It Is
Segment Breakdown
How It Works Under the Hood
On-Disk Data Sources
Graceful Degradation
Dashboard Sidecar
Customization
Status Line
While VibeCrew runs, a persistent status line at the bottom of your Claude Code terminal shows real-time session state. It updates after every assistant message at zero token cost — it's powered by a bash script, not the model.
&#9632;
What it is
A single ANSI-colored line rendered by statusline.sh. Claude Code pipes session JSON to the script's stdin on every assistant turn, and the script combines that with on-disk state files to produce a compact, color-coded status readout.
&#10003;
What problem it solves
Without the status line, you'd have to run /status repeatedly to check context usage, cost, and active feature. The status line gives you continuous visibility without spending tokens or interrupting your workflow.
Opus 4.6 ▓▓▓▓░░░░░░ 38% | $0.42 | auth-flow · Code | ↑85+ | 12m | ⟳0
Segment Breakdown
Seven segments, left to right:
SegmentExampleWhat It Shows
ModelOpus 4.6The Claude model powering the current session. Parsed from the session JSON that Claude Code pipes to the script on every turn.
Context Bar▓▓▓▓░░░░░░ 38%A 10-character progress bar visualizing context window usage. Each ▓ block represents 10% of the 200k-token window. Color-coded: green at &le;45%, yellow at 46&ndash;55%, and red above 55%. This is the most critical indicator — when it turns red, consider running /compact or /handoff to free space before the model starts losing earlier context.
Session Cost$0.42Cumulative API cost in USD for the current session. Helps you track spend in real time rather than waiting for a billing dashboard. The cost guardrail hook fires warnings at configurable thresholds independently, but the status line gives you a continuous readout.
Feature · Phaseauth-flow · CodeThe active feature name (truncated to 16 characters) and its current phase in the Tier 2 cycle: Plan, Design, Code, Test, Review, or Docs. During Tier 1, this shows foundation · Tier-1. If no project is initialized, it displays no project. Read from .vibecrew/state.json on disk.
Vibe Score↑85+The session's quality score (0&ndash;150) with a trend suffix: + means the score is improving across sessions, - means declining. Read from the latest score file in .vibecrew/scores/. When no score exists yet, displays ↑--.
Duration12mTotal elapsed session time in minutes. Shows <1m for sessions under 60 seconds. Useful for gauging how long an autonomous run has been going.
Compactions⟳0Number of /compact operations in the current session. Each compaction compresses the conversation to reclaim context window space. A rising number signals a long or context-heavy session. Read from .vibecrew/sessions/.
How It Works Under the Hood
Claude Code supports a statusLine setting in settings.json that points to a bash script. On every assistant turn, Claude Code pipes a JSON object to the script's stdin containing the current model, context window stats, cost, and timing data. The script parses this with jq, reads project state files from .vibecrew/, and outputs a single ANSI-colored line.
Configuration
The plugin's settings.json includes this entry, which Claude Code reads automatically:
stdin JSON Schema
This is the JSON object that Claude Code pipes to statusline.sh on every turn:
On-Disk Data Sources
The script combines piped data with on-disk reads:
Data SourceWhat It Provides
stdin JSONModel name, context percentage, session cost, elapsed time
.vibecrew/state.jsonActive feature name and current phase
.vibecrew/scores/score-*.jsonLatest Vibe Score and trend direction
.vibecrew/sessions/session-*.jsonCompaction count for the current session
Graceful Degradation
The status line never breaks your terminal. If jq is missing, it displays just VibeCrew. If .vibecrew/ doesn't exist, project-specific fields show placeholder values (no project, ↑--, ⟳0). The script always exits with code 0, regardless of parse errors.
Dashboard Sidecar
As a side effect, the status line script writes the raw session JSON to .vibecrew/live-session.json using an atomic move operation. The Vibe Dashboard reads this file to display real-time session metrics in the browser without any additional polling or API calls.
Customization
The status line script is fully customizable. You can modify statusline.sh directly to change colors, add segments, or remove fields you don't need. Alternatively, point the statusLine.command setting to your own script — as long as it reads JSON from stdin and outputs a single line to stdout, Claude Code will display it.

## Sub-Agents

Sub-Agents
Instead of one AI doing everything, VibeCrew splits work across specialized agents — like a real development team with planners, builders, testers, and reviewers. Most agents run on Opus, the most powerful model available. This is intentional: while Opus costs more per task and takes longer, the higher quality output means significantly less rework. Getting it right the first time saves more time and money than running a cheaper model that needs multiple correction rounds. Fast, mechanical tasks (routing, running shell commands) use Haiku, and template-driven output like documentation uses Sonnet.
&#9632;
What they are
AI specialists with scoped tool access, model selection, and turn budgets. Most run on Opus (the most capable model) because planning, coding, security, and analysis are tasks where mistakes are expensive to fix later. Haiku handles fast mechanical work, and Sonnet handles documentation.
&#10003;
What problem they solve
A single AI context window fills up fast when researching, coding, and testing in one session. Worktree agents offload expensive research into isolated contexts — only the distilled output enters your main session, saving thousands of tokens.
Agent Reference
Opus (complex reasoning)
Haiku (fast tasks)
Sonnet (documentation)

## Templates

Templates
Templates are the scaffolding blueprints VibeCrew uses to create consistent, well-structured artifacts across every project. From the initial VISION.md to test configs and session logs, every file that VibeCrew generates starts from a template. This ensures consistency, reduces agent token cost (no need to invent formats from scratch), and makes outputs predictable.
&#9632;
What they are
Template files in the templates/ directory: Markdown documents, JSON schemas, test configs, CI/CD pipelines, and a full VitePress documentation site scaffold. Agents fill in project-specific content while the structure stays consistent.
&#10003;
What problem they solve
Without templates, agents would invent different file formats each session — inconsistent backlog schemas, varying session log structures, and unpredictable CLAUDE.md layouts. Templates guarantee that every artifact works with every script, hook, and dashboard component.
Tier 1 Foundation Templates
These templates drive the /new-project workflow. Each foundation step produces a file from its template, filled with project-specific content by the responsible agent.
TemplateOutputCreated ByWhat It Defines
VISION.md.template
VISION.md
Orchestrator
Product vision, target audience, core value proposition, success metrics, and project scope.
design-system.css.template
design-system.css
Design Discovery or Import
CSS custom properties: colors, typography, spacing, radius, shadows, breakpoints — the design token file.
design-brief.md.template
design-brief.md
Design Discovery or Import
Rationale for design decisions — why these colors, fonts, and styles. Agents reference this during feature development.
tdr.md.template
TDR.md
Stack Scout
Technology Decision Record: framework, database, auth, hosting, testing, CI, with Token Impact Assessment for each choice.
roadmap.md.template
ROADMAP.md
Orchestrator
Feature roadmap with priority phases, dependencies, and estimated complexity.
CLAUDE.md.template
CLAUDE.md
Orchestrator
Project-level AI rules: conventions, constraints, architecture patterns, and session learnings. Kept under 200 lines.
State & Config Templates
Created during /setup to initialize the .vibecrew/ runtime directory. These define the JSON schemas that scripts, hooks, and the dashboard all rely on.
TemplateOutputWhat It Defines
config.json.template
.vibecrew/config.json
Terminal preference, notifications, user profile dimensions, cost thresholds, MCP server toggles.
state.json.template
.vibecrew/state.json
Foundation completion flags, active feature, current phase, feature history.

.vibecrew/backlog.json
Feature specs with Kanban columns, priority, complexity, acceptance criteria, and dependencies.
gamification.json.template
.vibecrew/gamification.json
XP, level, badge definitions, skill tree, streak tracking, challenge completions.
Testing & Quality Templates
Scaffolded into the project when the corresponding testing command is first used. Each template follows best practices for its test framework.
TemplateOutputWhat It Configures
vitest.config.ts.template

Structured JSON schemas for every type of report VibeCrew generates. These ensure consistent machine-readable output that the dashboard and scripts can parse.

## Testing Strategy

Testing Strategy
VibeCrew provides testing commands for your project code and includes its own comprehensive
test suite for the plugin's bash scripts. This page covers both.
&#9874;
Project Testing
4 slash commands for TDD, E2E, accessibility, and performance testing in your project.
&#9939;
Plugin Test Suite
Comprehensive unit and integration tests validating VibeCrew's own scripts.
Testing Your Project
VibeCrew provides 4 testing commands that work on your project code. Each integrates with the Vibe Score — running these commands earns bonuses, skipping them incurs deductions.
CommandToolWhat It Does
/tdd
Vitest / Jest
Red-green-refactor cycle. Writes ONE failing test, implements minimum code to pass, refactors, and commits. Produces a Discipline Score (0&ndash;10) measuring TDD adherence.
/e2e
Playwright
Scaffolds Page Object Model, generates spec files with accessibility-first locators, and runs with trace-on-failure for debugging.
/a11y
axe-core
WCAG 2.1 AA audit: automated axe scan, keyboard navigation checklist, ARIA validation. Saves a JSON report to the project.
/perf-test
k6
Load, stress, spike, and soak test profiles. Configures thresholds and reports p95/p99 latency, throughput, and error rates.
&#9888;
Project tests, not plugin tests
These commands test your application code. The section below covers VibeCrew's own internal test suite.
TDD Rationalization Resistance
The /tdd command includes built-in resistance to common reasons for skipping test-driven development. When the agent detects &ldquo;red flag&rdquo; phrases (like &ldquo;I&rsquo;ll add tests later&rdquo; or &ldquo;this is too simple to test&rdquo;), it stops and returns to the Red phase. The Iron Law: write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.
Nyquist Test Coverage Mapping
Before the Code phase begins, VibeCrew maps existing test coverage to acceptance criteria via map-test-coverage.sh. Criteria without matching tests become Wave 0 tasks — test scaffolding tasks inserted at the beginning of the plan, establishing the red-green-refactor starting point before any implementation.
StepWhat Happens
DetectIdentifies test framework (vitest, jest, playwright, cypress, bats) from config files
MapSearches existing test files for keyword matches against each acceptance criterion
GapFlags criteria with no matching test file as coverage gaps
Wave 0Generates test scaffolding tasks for each gap (create test file with failing test)
Wave 0 tasks go before implementation tasks in the plan. This is advisory — it never blocks plan completion. If no test framework is detected, VibeCrew notes it and skips.
Plugin Test Suite
VibeCrew's bash scripts form complex workflow chains. Unit tests validate individual
scripts in isolation. Integration tests validate the chains compose correctly — catching
the category of bugs that only appear when script A's output becomes script B's input.
All tests run in isolated temp directories with mocked external tools — zero network, zero side effects.
Testing Flow
How tests flow through the system, from development to CI to regression feedback.
<MermaidDiagram chart={`flowchart TD
DEV["Developer writes code"] --> UNIT["Unit Tests"]
DEV --> INT["Integration Tests"]
UNIT --> CI["CI Pipelineubuntu + macOS matrix"]
INT --> CI
CI --> PASS{"All pass?"}
PASS -->|Yes| MERGE["Merge to main"]
PASS -->|No| FIX["Fix failures"]
FIX --> DEV
MERGE --> WRAP["/wrap session"]
WRAP --> DETECT["detect-fix-commits.shScan for fix: commits"]
DETECT --> REGTEST{"Has testchanges?"}
REGTEST -->|No| SKELETON["generate-regression-test.shCreate test skeleton"]
SKELETON --> SCORE["-5 Vibe Score"]
REGTEST -->|Yes| OK["No deduction"]
style UNIT fill:#bfb,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px
style INT fill:#bbf,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px
style CI fill:#ffd,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px
style SKELETON fill:#fde8e8,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px
style OK fill:#e8fde8,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px`}
caption="Full testing flow: unit and integration tests feed CI, /wrap detects fix commits without regression tests."
/>
Testing Pyramid
Two automated tiers plus manual validation for complete coverage.
<MermaidDiagram chart={`flowchart TD
A["Manual Testing(Full Claude Code session)"] --> B
B["Integration Tests(workflow chains)"] --> C
C["Unit Tests(individual scripts)"]
style A fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px
style B fill:#bbf,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px
style C fill:#bfb,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px`}
caption="Test pyramid: unit tests form the base, integration tests validate chains, manual testing covers full sessions."
/>

How Tests Are Isolated
Every test creates an ephemeral project directory, runs in isolation, and cleans up after itself.
<MermaidDiagram chart={`flowchart LR
A["mktemp -d"] --> B["git init"]
B --> C["Create .vibecrew/"]
C --> D["Run test"]
D --> E["rm -rf"]
style A fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#333
style E fill:#fde8e8,stroke:#333`}
caption="Test lifecycle: create temp dir, initialize git, create state files, run test, clean up."
/>
Mocking Strategy
External tools are always mocked. Internal scripts run for real in integration tests.
LayerWhat's MockedHow
External CLIs
gh, glab, node, npm
mock_command() — executable stub prepended to PATH
Package managers
bun, pnpm, yarn
Same PATH prepend pattern
System tools
terminal-notifier, timeout
Same pattern
File system
None — uses real temp dirs
mktemp -d with cleanup in teardown
Git
Real git in temp repos
git init in setup, real commits when needed
Internal scripts
Not mocked in integration tests
Scripts call each other directly
Running Tests
The test runner supports three modes via a single entry point.
tests/run-tests.sh              # All tests (unit + integration)
tests/run-tests.sh unit         # Unit tests only
tests/run-tests.sh integration  # Integration tests only
Regression Test Feedback Loop
When bug fixes are committed without accompanying tests, VibeCrew automatically generates
regression test skeletons to close the loop.
<MermaidDiagram chart={`flowchart LR
A["fix: commitdetected"] --> B{"Has testchanges?"}
B -->|No| C["detect-fix-commits.sh"]
C --> D["generate-regression-test.sh"]
D --> E["Skeleton committedwith skip marker"]
B -->|Yes| F["No action needed"]
style A fill:#fde8e8,stroke:#333
style E fill:#e8fde8,stroke:#333
style F fill:#e8fde8,stroke:#333`}
caption="Fix commits without tests trigger automatic skeleton generation during /wrap."
/>
The Vibe Score applies a -5 deduction per fix commit without a regression test.
After 3+ sessions with uncovered fixes, the Performance Coach proposes a CLAUDE.md mutation
enforcing TDD-style bug fixing.
CI Pipeline
GitHub Actions runs two parallel jobs on push/PR to main.
JobSuiteSpeedTimeout
unit-tests
tests/*.bats
~15-20min
30min
integration-tests
tests/integration/*.bats
~2-5min
10min
Both run on ubuntu-latest + macos-latest matrix with fail-fast: false.

## Vibe Dashboard

On This Page
What is the Vibe Dashboard
How to Start It
Dashboard Tabs
CLI Alternatives
Data Flow
Production Build
Troubleshooting
Overview
What is the Vibe Dashboard
The Vibe Dashboard is a VitePress-powered documentation site scaffolded into every VibeCrew project during /setup. It lives in your project's docs/ folder and provides a browser-based interface for browsing development metrics, managing your feature backlog, and editing project settings.
The dashboard reads live data from .vibecrew/ — the same JSON files that power the CLI commands. It includes 10 tabs: a project overview (About), a getting-started guide, a Kanban board, session statistics, Vibe Score trends, a session logbook, test coverage, achievements, a release timeline, and a settings editor.
This page documents the per-project Vibe Dashboard that gets scaffolded into your project. It's separate from the VibeCrew companion documentation site (the one you're reading right now).
Getting Started
How to Start It
Launch the dashboard with a single command from your project root. The script auto-installs dependencies if needed and opens your browser automatically:
The script checks for missing node_modules, runs npm install if necessary, starts the VitePress dev server, and opens http://localhost:5173 in your default browser. The dashboard hot-reloads when .vibecrew/ data changes.
Open a separate terminal tab for the dashboard. It runs on its own port and doesn't interfere with your application's dev server. In Warp, use a split pane or a dedicated tab.
Features
Dashboard Tabs
The dashboard ships with 10 tabs. Each tab reads from specific .vibecrew/ JSON files via VitePress data loaders.
About
A project overview page sourced from your foundation artifacts:
Hero — Project name, tagline, and description from VISION.md
Target Audience — Who the project is for
Problems Solved — What problems it addresses
Feature Showcase — Grid of completed features with links to feature docs
Tech Stack — Technology stack summary from TDR.md
Dev Server — Table of npm scripts with auto-update explanation
Data source: VISION.md, TDR.md, package.json, .vibecrew/backlog.json
Guide
The default landing tab. Contains the same getting-started documentation that's scaffolded into docs/system/getting-started.md — a quick reference for setup, commands, and workflow.
Kanban Board
A 7-column interactive board showing every feature in your backlog across its workflow stages:
Ideas — Raw ideas captured via /idea or the + button on the dashboard
Planning — Features actively being planned (specs in progress)
Planned — Features with complete specs, ready to build
In Development — Currently being built by the Builder agent
Testing — Running tests and quality checks
Review — Code review in progress
Done — Feature complete, wrapped, and documented
Add ideas via the + button, drag cards between columns, click to edit specs, and launch Warp sessions with action buttons. A live session bar shows real-time Claude Code status (model, context usage, cost).
Data source: .vibecrew/backlog.json
Session Statistics
Aggregate metrics across all your development sessions:
Total sessions — Number of completed sessions
Average Vibe Score — Your mean score across all sessions
Total tokens — Input + output token usage
Estimated cost — Cumulative API cost
Data source: .vibecrew/sessions/*.json
Trends
Time-series visualizations of your development patterns:
Vibe Score line chart — Score trajectory across sessions
Token breakdown — Input vs. output tokens per session
Agent activity — Which agents ran and how often
Data source: .vibecrew/scores/*.json
Session Logbook
A per-session drill-down that complements the aggregate Stats and Trends views. Each session expands into a detail panel showing:
Task Summary — What was accomplished in the session
Vibe Score Breakdown — Score with deductions (red) and bonuses (green) as pills
Token Usage — Input, cache creation, cache read, output, cost, and cache hit rate
Context Window — Peak usage percentage and compaction count
Agents Used — Color-coded chips for each agent invoked
Test Results — Total, passed, failed, and coverage percentage
Files Modified — Collapsible list with insertions/deletions per file
Commits — Hash and message for each commit
Coaching — Suggestions from the Vibe Score analysis
Sessions can be filtered by feature and sorted by date. Scores are joined by session_id.
Data source: .vibecrew/sessions/*.json, .vibecrew/scores/*.json
Coverage
Quality metrics at a glance:
Test coverage gauge — Percentage of code covered by tests
Feature delivery progress — Completed features vs. total backlog
Achievements
The gamification system rendered visually:
Level & XP — Your current level and experience points
Badges — Earned badges with unlock conditions
Skill radar — Radar chart of your development skills
Streak calendar — Daily activity streak tracking
Data source: .vibecrew/gamification.json
Releases
A vertical timeline of all project releases created by /wrap and /release:
Version badge — Version number and release date
Change sections — Grouped by type: Features, Fixes, Refactors, Docs, Other (only non-empty sections shown)
Commit stats — Total commits, files changed, insertions, and deletions
Data source: .vibecrew/releases/*.json
Settings
A browser-based editor for .vibecrew/config.json. You can modify:
User profile — Role, code literacy, autonomy, verbosity, and other profile dimensions
Notifications — Toggle notification delivery and sound
Cost limits — Set per-session and per-feature cost caps
MCP servers — Enable or disable optional MCP integrations
Agent behavior — Adjust agent-specific settings
Gamification — Toggle scoring, achievements, and XP display
When running npm run docs:dev, interactive features (adding ideas, dragging cards, editing specs, saving settings) write changes directly to .vibecrew/ files. In a static production build (npm run docs:build), the board renders read-only.
Terminal Equivalents
CLI Alternatives
Every dashboard tab has a terminal equivalent. If you prefer staying in the CLI, these commands show the same data:
Dashboard TabCLI CommandWhat It Shows
Kanban / Stats/statusFeature backlog overview, session count, current feature
Stats / Trends/costToken usage, API costs, per-session breakdown
Achievements/achievementsLevel, XP, badges, streaks, challenges
Settings (profile)/profileEdit user profile dimensions interactively
Coverage/checkRun tests, lint, type-check, and see coverage
Logbook/status + /costSession history and per-session cost breakdown
Releases/releaseCreate releases and view release notes
About/statusProject overview and foundation status
Architecture
Data Flow
The dashboard reads data through a simple pipeline:
.vibecrew/*.json          # Raw data written by VibeCrew agents
|
VitePress data loaders      # .data.ts files that read and transform JSON
|
Vue components             # Render charts, tables, cards, forms
|
Browser                    # Hot-reloads when data files change
Data loaders run at build time (for static builds) or on each page load (in dev mode). In dev mode, VitePress watches the .vibecrew/ directory and triggers hot-reloads when any JSON file changes — so running /wrap in a Claude Code session updates the dashboard in real time.
In dev mode, the dashboard also provides API endpoints for CRUD operations and uses Vite's built-in WebSocket for real-time push updates when .vibecrew/ files change.
All data lives in flat JSON files inside .vibecrew/. There's no database, no backend server, and no external dependencies beyond VitePress itself. The dashboard is a pure static site that reads local files.
Deployment
Production Build
To generate a static HTML version of the dashboard:
The output goes to docs/.vitepress/dist/. You can deploy this to any static hosting provider (Vercel, Netlify, GitHub Pages) to share project metrics with your team.
A production build captures a point-in-time snapshot of your .vibecrew/ data. This is useful for sprint reviews, stakeholder updates, or archiving project history.
Help
Troubleshooting
Dashboard shows empty/no data
The dashboard reads from .vibecrew/ JSON files that are created as you work. If you haven't completed any sessions yet:
Run /new-project to create the project foundation
Build at least one feature with /new-feature "name"
Close the session with /wrap — this writes session data, scores, and updates the backlog
After your first /wrap, all dashboard tabs will populate with data.
Port 5173 is already in use
If another dev server is using port 5173, VitePress will automatically try the next available port (5174, 5175, etc.). Check the terminal output for the actual URL. You can also specify a port explicitly:
Drag-and-drop not working
Interactive features (drag-and-drop, adding ideas, editing cards) only work when running the dev server. Static builds render the board read-only.
Settings changes don't persist
The Settings tab can only write to .vibecrew/config.json when VitePress is running in dev mode (npm run docs:dev). If you're viewing a static build, Settings shows a read-only view with copyable JSON that you can paste into .vibecrew/config.json manually.
Hot-reload isn't working
Make sure you're running the dev server (npm run docs:dev), not viewing a static build
Check that .vibecrew/ is in the same project root where you started VitePress
Try restarting the dev server — VitePress occasionally needs a restart after major file structure changes

Tips: What Users Say vs What Agents Build
VibeCrew agents translate plain language into precise component vocabulary. Here are common examples:
What you say
What gets built
"A dropdown for picking a country"Combobox (type-ahead search with 200+ items)
"A popup to confirm deleting"Alert Dialog (traps focus, requires explicit choice)
"A sidebar with links"Sidebar + Navigation Menu (keyboard navigable, collapsible)
"A table with sorting"Data Table (sortable headers, pagination, filterable)
"A toast message"Sonner (auto-dismissing, accessible live region)
"A settings page"Tabs + Form + Switch (progressive disclosure, instant toggles)
"A like button"Button + Optimistic UI (instant update, silent retry on failure)
"A dashboard"Card grid + Chart + Skeleton Loading + SWR (fast perceived load)
"A search bar"Combobox + Debounced Search (waits until you stop typing)
"A list of 500 items"Data Table + List Virtualization (only renders visible rows)
"Work on mobile"Mobile-First Layout + Touch Target Sizing + Responsive Navigation
"Handle errors gracefully"Error Boundary + Custom 404/500 + Network Error Toast

Patterns.dev — Performance and rendering patterns for modern web apps

Inclusive Components — Heydon Pickering's guide to accessible component patterns

## Dark Patterns to Avoid

Dark Patterns to Avoid
Deceptive design patterns that manipulate users into unintended actions. VibeCrew agents detect and prevent these during design and code review. Each pattern includes detection guidance and ethical alternatives.
{categories.map((cat) => (
{categoryLabels[cat]}
))}
Ethical Design Checklist

)}

Ethical Design Checklist
Before shipping any feature involving consent, checkout, subscriptions, or user decisions, run through this 7-question cognitive walkthrough (adapted from NNGroup):
Equal weight test — Do all options (accept/reject, subscribe/skip, buy/cancel) have equal visual prominence?
No surprises test — Is the total cost visible from the first price display? Are all fees disclosed?
One-click reversal test — Can the user undo their action (unsubscribe, cancel, opt out) as easily as they did it?
Neutral language test — Are decline options written in neutral tone without guilt or shame?
Real data test — Are all numbers (stock counts, user counts, reviews, timers) backed by real data?
Respect decline test — When a user says "no," does the system remember and stop asking?
Transparency test — Would you be comfortable if a regulator reviewed this UI flow?
Tips: What Users Say vs What Gets Built
What you sayWhat gets built
"Cookie consent"Equal-weight Accept/Reject buttons + granular settings + consent logging
"Free trial signup"Clear conversion terms + pre-charge reminder email + one-click cancellation
"Pricing page"Honest comparison table + all fees visible + no pre-selected premium tier
"Newsletter popup"Single non-intrusive prompt + neutral decline + dismissal persistence
Related Pages
Legal & Compliance — Legal patterns including consent asymmetry, pre-checked options, and hidden subscription regulations
Business Patterns — Ethical conversion and trust patterns that work without manipulation
Form Patterns — Accessible, user-respecting form design
Sources & Further Reading
deceptive.design — Harry Brignull's comprehensive dark pattern taxonomy and hall of shame
Nielsen Norman Group — Dark pattern research and ethical design guidelines
FTC: Bringing Dark Patterns to Light — US Federal Trade Commission enforcement report
GDPR.eu — Cookie consent requirements under GDPR and ePrivacy
CookieYes — Dark patterns in cookie consent and how to avoid them
